questions.q: According to moral relativism, what determines whether an action is obligatory for a member of a culture?
options: The basic moral norms of that culture
The objective moral facts that apply to all cultures
The individual's personal conscience
The laws of the nation-state
The universal principles of human reason
questions.explain: MR defines obligation entirely by reference to the culture's basic moral norms. The objective facts perspective belongs to moral objectivism, not MR.

questions.q: Which statement best captures the core difference between moral relativism (MR) and moral objectivism (MO)?
options: MR concerns only individual beliefs, while MO concerns only group beliefs
MR says moral standards are culture-dependent; MO says at least some moral norms are culture-independent
MR allows cultural variation, while MO does not
MR applies only to major moral norms, while MO applies to all moral norms
MR requires universal agreement, while MO permits disagreement
questions.explain: The fundamental distinction is about where moral standards come from: MR derives them from cultural norms, MO from culture-independent facts.

questions.q: What does the context sensitivity thesis claim?
options: Different cultures have fundamentally incompatible moral codes
What is right or wrong often depends on one's circumstances, including cultural facts
Moral norms must be applied universally without regard to context
Culture is insensitive to moral principles
Context is morally irrelevant to evaluating actions
questions.explain: CS says context affects what one ought to do. This is distinct from MR because CS is compatible with universal underlying principles.

questions.q: Why is the drowning child example used to illustrate context sensitivity?
options: It shows that swimmers have special obligations that non-swimmers lack
It demonstrates how a universal principle can yield different verdicts based on non-moral factual differences
It proves that moral norms are entirely relative to culture
It shows that context is irrelevant to moral evaluation
It illustrates that children deserve more moral protection than adults
questions.explain: The example shows one objective principle producing different verdicts based on factual differences — not a difference in moral standards.

questions.q: According to the lecture, does moral relativism necessarily entail moral diversity?
options: Yes, MR always requires that cultures disagree on basic norms
No, MR is compatible with universal agreement if those norms are set by cultural convention
Yes, because all cultures must have different moral codes by definition
No, because moral diversity is a descriptive claim, not a normative one
Yes, but only in modern pluralistic societies
questions.explain: Even if all cultures adopted identical norms, MR could be true if those norms were set by convention rather than objective fact.

questions.q: What is the main problem with the first version of the Anthropologist's Argument?
options: It assumes all cultures agree on moral norms
It conflates disagreement in belief with disagreement over objective fact, and fails to distinguish nonfundamental from fundamental disagreements
It requires evidence that is impossible to gather
It assumes moral progress is always possible
It bases morality on empirical facts rather than norms
questions.explain: P2 errs by assuming disagreement implies no correct answer, and P1 ignores that surface disagreements may rest on different non-moral beliefs.

questions.q: In the capital punishment disagreement, why would disagreement about beneficial consequences be classified as nonfundamental?
options: Because it is possible to resolve through discussion
Because both parties accept the same basic moral norm and disagree only on non-moral empirical facts
Because capital punishment is not a serious moral issue
Because one party has mistaken beliefs
Because objective moral norms do not apply
questions.explain: Nonfundamental disagreement exists when both parties share the same basic norm but differ on empirical facts.

questions.q: Which disagreement would count as fundamental rather than nonfundamental?
options: Disagreement about whether capital punishment deters crime
Disagreement about whether rehabilitation or retribution is the proper purpose of punishment
Disagreement about how many years a sentence should be
Disagreement about which crimes deserve capital punishment
Disagreement about whether judges should have discretion
questions.explain: A fundamental disagreement is at the level of basic moral norms themselves — not at the level of empirical fact.

questions.q: What does the 'chicken pull' case contribute to the Anthropologist's Argument Version 2?
options: It shows rationality alone cannot resolve all moral disagreements
It suggests that some moral disagreements have a correct answer independent of cultural convention
It demonstrates that animals deserve the same moral consideration as humans
It proves that moral objectivism is incompatible with cultural diversity
It illustrates that cultural practices always reflect deeper moral principles
questions.explain: Even when someone shares all non-moral beliefs, an objectivist can insist the person is mistaken — suggesting moral facts exist independently.

questions.q: Why does the consistency problem pose a challenge to moral relativism?
options: It shows all cultures must agree on at least some norms
Because a person belonging to multiple cultures with conflicting norms would face contradictory obligations
Because moral relativism denies any moral norms are universal
Because it is impossible to determine what counts as a culture
Because some people have inconsistent personal beliefs
questions.explain: MR yields that an action could be simultaneously right and wrong for one person.

questions.q: What makes the determinacy problem a practical challenge for moral relativism?
options: It requires all cultures adopt the same moral norms
Because without a clear criterion for what counts as a culture, one cannot specify which norms determine right and wrong
Because cultures are constantly changing their moral standards
Because MR requires agreement with objective facts
Because most people do not understand relativistic thinking
questions.explain: If 'culture' is undefined, then MR cannot function as a decision procedure for moral action.

questions.q: How does the problem of intercultural evaluation challenge moral relativism?
options: It shows cultural practices are always morally superior to individual ones
It demonstrates one cannot rationally criticize another culture's practices if that culture's norms set the standard
It proves all cultures hold the same basic moral views
It suggests moral progress is only possible within a single culture
It requires all moral standards be objective and universal
questions.explain: If a culture's basic norms set the ultimate standard, external criticism becomes meaningless under MR.

questions.q: What does the intracultural evaluation problem reveal about moral relativism?
options: That cultures are always morally improving
That claims about moral decline or progress within a culture become conceptually incoherent if the culture's norms always set the standard
That old moral codes were superior to modern ones
That individual moral beliefs cannot be criticized within a culture
That moral objectivism is the only coherent theory
questions.explain: If the old norms were the correct standard for their time, saying 'we've improved' becomes nonsensical under MR.

questions.q: Why is the moral reformer problem particularly damaging to moral relativism?
options: It shows reformers are always wrong about their proposals
Because it makes moral progress conceptually impossible — a reformer opposing their culture's norms is by definition wrong
Because it proves only objective moral standards can exist
Because reformers must accept their culture's norms
Because moral reformers create conflict within societies
questions.explain: Under unrestricted MR, the reformer who opposes their culture's norms is automatically wrong — yet we regard many reformers as morally justified.

questions.q: How does the problem of internal support relate to explanatory power?
options: Internal support requires all cultures agree on moral norms
Both arise when MR cannot justify why an individual's moral judgment (e.g., Nazi racism is wrong) seems correct
They show moral objectivism must be true
They demonstrate moral progress is always beneficial
They reveal moral disagreements are always resolvable
questions.explain: When MR cannot explain why a moral reformer's opposition seems justified, it fails both internal support and explanatory power.

questions.q: What is the defining characteristic of restricted moral relativism (RMR)?
options: It abandons cultural variation entirely
It allows cultural variation only within universal constraints reflecting morality's functions and human nature
It denies objective moral standards exist
It claims all moral norms are relative to individuals rather than cultures
It rejects the possibility of moral progress
questions.explain: RMR preserves cultural variation but imposes universal constraints — avoiding 'anything goes' relativism.

questions.q: Which would be a culture-independent constraint under restricted moral relativism?
options: The requirement that all cultures adopt identical moral codes
That moral norms must reflect the functions of morality and facts about human nature, including satisfying physical needs and enabling intimacy
That moral standards must be based on religious doctrine
That all moral disagreements can be resolved empirically
That cultures must abandon their traditional practices
questions.explain: RMR's universal constraints are grounded in morality's functions and human capacities/needs, not specific cultural prescriptions.

questions.q: According to the lecture, which norm does the interpersonal function of morality yield under RMR?
options: That all individuals must conform to cultural majority opinion
A norm of reciprocity requiring the return of good for good, along with encouragement of other-regarding behavior and personal freedom
That cultures must prioritize individual autonomy above all other values
That moral norms must be based on rational self-interest
That all moral disagreements reflect fundamental value conflicts
questions.explain: The interpersonal function generates norms promoting mutual benefit and respect, including reciprocity and personal freedom.

questions.q: How is restricted moral relativism pluralistic?
options: It allows all moral codes to be equally correct regardless of content
Multiple moral codes can be equally correct if they both satisfy the universal constraints
It denies any moral standards are binding
It claims each individual can create their own moral code
It requires all cultures eventually converge on the same norms
questions.explain: RMR is pluralistic because different codes can both be correct if they satisfy universal constraints — not 'anything goes.'

questions.q: Why is unrestricted moral relativism self-defeating regarding tolerance?
options: Because it requires all cultures to be tolerant
Because if moral standards are set by each culture's norms, a culture requiring interference with others cannot be told it is wrong to interfere
Because it denies tolerance has any moral value
Because it makes moral progress impossible
Because it assumes all moral disagreements are fundamental
questions.explain: If a culture's norms set its moral standard, the relativist cannot consistently condemn interference — so MR cannot ground tolerance.

questions.q: According to the lecture, how does restricted moral relativism resolve the tension between relativism and tolerance?
options: By abandoning cultural variation
By grounding tolerance in the universal constraints that apply to all adequate moral codes
By requiring all cultures to adopt identical values
By making tolerance culturally relative
By asserting tolerance is not a genuine moral value
questions.explain: RMR can mandate tolerance by making it stem from the universal constraints on adequate morality.

questions.q: Is moral objectivism necessarily incompatible with tolerance?
options: Yes, because objectivism requires imposing universal standards
No, tolerance can be grounded in objective moral principles just as it can in RMR
Yes, because objectivism denies cultural variation
No, because all moral objectivists reject cultural practices
Yes, because objectivism requires uniform moral codes globally
questions.explain: Accepting objective moral standards does not automatically lead to intolerance — tolerance can be an objective principle.

questions.q: What is the key distinction the lecture draws between describing moral beliefs and making normative moral claims?
options: Describing beliefs is objective while making normative claims is subjective
Moral relativism is about normative claims (facts differ), not merely descriptive disagreement in belief
Normative claims are always more important than descriptive ones
Descriptive and normative claims always conflict with each other
Both describe the same underlying reality
questions.explain: MR makes the normative claim that moral facts differ by culture — not merely that beliefs differ.

questions.q: How can the same basic moral norm lead to different verdicts across cultures under moral objectivism?
options: If the underlying moral principle is really relative rather than objective
If non-moral factual beliefs differ (as illustrated by the drowning child case) while the universal principle remains constant
If different cultures have fundamentally incompatible basic norms
If the culture's norms override objective standards
If moral standards change over time
questions.explain: One universal principle generates different verdicts based on factual differences, compatible with objectivism.

questions.q: What assumption does the Anthropologist's Argument Version 1 make that the lecture questions?
options: That all cultures must agree on some moral norms
That disagreement in moral belief necessarily means there are no objective moral facts
That cultures are incapable of change
That moral norms are based entirely on empirical facts
That objectivism requires all cultures to be identical
questions.explain: The argument assumes disagreement entails no objective fact, but the earth-shape case shows disagreement can exist even with clear objective answers.

questions.q: Why is it significant that MD (moral diversity) does not entail MR (moral relativism)?
options: Because it shows MR must be false
Because it reveals observed moral disagreement does not automatically establish relativism — objective standards could underlie cultural differences
Because it proves all cultures share basic moral norms
Because it demonstrates context sensitivity is objective
Because it shows all moral norms are culture-independent
questions.explain: If MD doesn't entail MR, showing cultural disagreement is insufficient to prove relativism.

questions.q: According to the lecture, what would make a moral disagreement resolvable?
options: If it involves only subjective preferences
If it rests on differing non-moral factual beliefs that can be examined empirically
If both parties accept the same cultural norms
If the disagreement is about consequences rather than principles
If one culture is more developed than the other
questions.explain: Nonfundamental disagreements are resolvable because they involve shared basic norms but different factual beliefs.

questions.q: Which version of the Anthropologist's Argument is stronger according to the lecture?
options: Version 1, because it requires only observing moral differences
Version 2, because it specifies that fundamental disagreements are widespread and rationally irresolvable, providing a better explanation for why objective norms don't exist
Version 1, because it avoids making empirical claims about disagreements
Version 2, because it directly proves moral objectivism is false
Neither version provides any support for relativism
questions.explain: Version 2 is stronger because it attempts to rule out nonfundamental disagreements and grounds the conclusion in inference to the best explanation.

questions.q: What do the exam traps in this lecture consistently emphasize?
options: That moral objectivism is obviously correct
That common errors involve conflating descriptive claims with normative ones, or context-sensitivity with relativism itself
That moral relativism provides strong support for tolerance
That all moral disagreements are fundamental
That cultures are incapable of moral improvement
questions.explain: Exam traps highlight confusions between describing variation and normative claims, and between context-sensitivity and relativism.

questions.q: What does the lecture say about the relationship between nonfundamental disagreements and empirical resolvability?
options: They cannot be resolved even with complete empirical information
Nonfundamental disagreements can be resolved by examining empirical evidence because they rest on shared basic norms but different factual beliefs
All disagreements are equally difficult to resolve empirically
Empirical evidence is irrelevant to resolving any moral disagreements
Only fundamental disagreements can be resolved empirically
questions.explain: Nonfundamental disagreements involve shared norms but differ on empirical facts — investigation can settle these questions.

questions.q: In Natural Law Theory, what is the key distinction between the descriptive and normative senses?
options: Descriptive: moral laws; normative: regularities
Descriptive: divine will; normative: legislation
Descriptive: animals; normative: humans only
Descriptive: observed regularities; normative: prescriptions for behavior based on human nature
Descriptive: relative; normative: absolute
questions.explain: Normative laws prescribe conduct based on human nature; descriptive laws are factual.

questions.q: Which lists the three interlocking components of Aquinas NLT?
options: Virtue ethics, deontology, consequentialism
Divine command, natural law, human reason
Intention, consequence, character
Autonomy, dignity, universal principles
Perfectionist theory, PDE, and moral absolutism
questions.explain: NLTs three core components are value perfectionism, PDE, and moral absolutism.

questions.q: For PDE to permit an action, what must be true?
options: Good effect numerically greater
Agent lacks negative motivation
Majority approves
Bad effect reversible
Not intrinsically wrong, bad effect not intended, proportionally grave reason
questions.explain: PDE requires all three conditions to be satisfied.

questions.q: How does NLT distinguish direct from indirect violation?
options: Direct: hinders good AND not justified by PDE; indirect: hinders but IS justified by PDE
Direct: intentional; indirect: unintentional
Direct: harms agent; indirect: harms others
Direct: permanent; indirect: temporary
They are synonymous
questions.explain: PDE is the dividing line between direct and indirect violations.

questions.q: What does Moral Absolutism assert?
options: Certain action-types always wrong, even with good results
All moral rules absolute without exception
No absolute moral rules exist
Absolute rules overridable by consequences
Only autonomy-rules matter
questions.explain: Moral Absolutism claims exceptionless prohibitions on certain action-types.

questions.q: How does NLT respond to pure consequentialism?
options: Rejects it: intentions matter in determining permissibility
Embraces consequentialism
Claims consequences irrelevant
Treats it as sole competitor
Argues conflicts unresolvable
questions.explain: NLT explicitly rejects consequentialism; intentions are morally relevant.

questions.q: For NLT right conduct, action is obligatory when:
options: Failing to perform results in direct violation of basic goods
Agent personally desires it
Conforms to cultural expectations
Maximizes overall utility
Majority approves
questions.explain: Obligatory actions are those whose omission results in direct violation.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, human value consists in:
options: Fulfilling purposes characteristic of rational agents
Accumulating material wealth
Obeying all laws and customs
Maximizing pleasure and minimizing pain
Gaining community approval
questions.explain: Aquinas perfectionism grounds value in fulfilling rational agent purposes.

questions.q: What does teleological worldview mean in perfectionism?
options: Morality determined by human feelings
All things have purposes; goodness in realising those purposes
Moral laws are human conventions
Physical world operates by mechanical causation
Gods commands determine morality
questions.explain: Aquinas teleological worldview holds all things have inherent purposes.

questions.q: The Problem of Moral Conflict in NLT arises because:
options: Moral truth is purely relative
Different basic goods clash, making fulfilling one seem to require violating another
Humans lack moral reasoning
Consequentialism is only framework
NLT has no resolution method
questions.explain: Moral conflicts arise when basic goods collide.

questions.q: In hysterectomy, why does PDE permit operation?
options: Saving mother is grave, not intrinsically wrong, childs death foreseen not intended
Mothers life worth more
Consent justifies any procedure
Child undeveloped
Utilitarian calculation favors more
questions.explain: All three PDE conditions satisfied in hysterectomy case.

questions.q: Why is active euthanasia wrong while pain medication permissible?
options: Active performed by physicians
Active directly intends killing; pain foresees but not intends, justified by PDE
Pain medication more effective
Active easier to detect
Pain always saves lives
questions.explain: Active intends death; pain aims at relief with death as side-effect.

questions.q: How does Value Perfectionism define goodness?
options: By market value
By obedience to God
Fully developing essential capacities
By extent of happiness
By conformity to social norms
questions.explain: VP states goodness consists in fully developing essential capacities.

questions.q: In PDE, what does non-intentionality require?
options: Agent not feel negative emotion
Agent act unconsciously
Bad effect not intended—neither as end nor as means
Bad effect not known
Agent must claim not to intend
questions.explain: Non-intentionality: bad effect not intended as end or means.

questions.q: In craniotomy, why does PDE NOT justify abortion?
options: Craniotomy has poor outcomes
Mother could decline
Childs death is means—not foreseen side-effect—violating non-intentionality
Doctors motive to save mother
Fetuses lack status
questions.explain: In craniotomy, childs death is means, violating non-intentionality.

questions.q: How does NLT analysis of self-defence illustrate absolutism?
options: Self-defence never permissible
Force permissible, but intending aggressors death still wrong
Absolutism only applies to defence
Self-defence obligatory
Aggressors forfeit protection
questions.explain: NLT permits force but maintains absolutism.

questions.q: Perfectionist theory defines state intrinsically bad when:
options: Requires effort prevent
Produces unhappiness
Violates legal standards
Hinders/destroys states perfecting human nature
Creates cultural conflict
questions.explain: Intrinsic badness grounded in hindering human perfection.

questions.q: According to NLT, four basic human goods are:
options: Pleasure, achievement, autonomy, acceptance
Health, wealth, happiness, security
Life, Procreation, Knowledge, Sociability
Power, wisdom, virtue, honor
Freedom, equality, justice, peace
questions.explain: NLT identifies exactly four basic goods.

questions.q: What does Harman argue about PDE and cognition?
options: PDE is purely religious
Divergent trolley intuitions suggest PDE innate to cognition
Trolley problem proves intuitions unreliable
All humans apply PDE correctly
PDE no connection to judgment
questions.explain: Harman argues trolley intuitions mirror PDEs non-intentionality.

questions.q: Fundamental Principle prescribes four basic goods:
options: Merely aspirational
Ranked hierarchically
Preserved/promoted; hindrance avoided
Pursued if majority approves
Balanced against freedom
questions.explain: Fundamental Principle is categorical: all carry genuine obligations.

questions.q: For PDEs non-intentionality, which true?
options: Only ultimate goal effects count
Only unforeseeable effects count
Both end and means effects prohibited
Agent conscious thoughts determine
Intention only religious
questions.explain: PDE prohibits intending evil as end OR means.

questions.q: In trolley bystander, why lever permissible?
options: Easier
Worker death foreseen side-effect, not means/intent, satisfies non-intentionality
Five lives worth more
No responsibility
Worker consented
questions.explain: Ones death unintended, mirrors PDEs non-intentionality.

questions.q: What is is-ought gap objection?
options: NLT confuses natural/supernatural
NLT ignores biological facts
Gap between humans/animals proves false
Cannot derive ought from is—logical problem in inference
Natural laws dont exist
questions.explain: Is-ought gap: facts alone cannot justify moral norms.

questions.q: Why footbridge case fails PDE?
options: Pushing violent
Man did not consent
Bridge public
One life cannot worth five
Mans body used as means; death not mere side-effect
questions.explain: Mans death necessary means, violates non-intentionality.

questions.q: How does circularity differ from is-ought?
options: Identical
Circularity logic; is-ought ethics
Circularity refutes; semantic
Is-ought: cant derive ought; circularity: identifying good presupposes value
Both refutations
questions.explain: Is-ought about logical form; circularity about content.

questions.q: What problem NOT fully resolved in NLTs conflict approach?
options: Whether goods conflict
Whether humans have obligations
Whether intentions matter
How to resolve conflicts—neither approach fully worked out
Whether aggressors have status
questions.explain: NLT offers two approaches but neither fully developed.

questions.q: What alternative value-basis replace perfectionism?
options: Consequentialist utility
Divine command
Preference satisfaction
Social contract
Welfare/well-being rather than perfection
questions.explain: Welfare/well-being presented as alternative within NLT.

questions.q: Is value-priority without perfectionism critique fatal?
options: Yes, disproves NLT
Proves consequentialism superior
Shows objective ethics impossible
No, raises question but doesn't refute core—could adopt alternative value account within framework
Shows conflicts unresolvable
questions.explain: Critique internal: change value-basis within NLT structure.

questions.q: Why might not all inclinations morally endorsed by NLT?
options: Humans irrational
Culture removes naturalness
Morality has no nature basis
All inclinations permissible
Natural inclinations like aggression/cruelty unendorsed—creates gap in derivation
questions.explain: Aggression/cruelty natural yet unendorsed, creating gap.

questions.q: Whats emphasized about four goods obligations?
options: Merely aspirational
Ranked strictly
Only three obligatory
Procreation permission
All four genuine obligations, not permissions
questions.explain: All four goods obligatory in NLT.

questions.q: According to the three theses of consequentialism, what relationship does value have to rightness?
options: Value is independent of the right, and rightness is derived from value facts
Rightness and value are mutually dependent and cannot be separated
Rightness determines value; value is a consequence of what is right
Value is a secondary concept derived from rules of right conduct
Rightness and value are entirely separate domains with no logical connection
questions.explain: The first thesis states that value is independent of the right and has explanatory priority—rightness is derived from value, not vice versa.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the four interlocking components of Classical Act Utilitarianism?
options: Maximising conception
Welfarism
Agent-based partiality
Universalism
Impartialism / Agent-neutrality
questions.explain: The four components are maximising, welfarism, universalism, and impartialism/agent-neutrality. Agent-based partiality is explicitly rejected.

questions.q: What is the defining characteristic of Ethical Hedonism in terms of intrinsic value?
options: Experiences of pleasure are the only items of intrinsic value with which ethics is concerned
Pleasure and pain are equally valuable in determining moral rightness
Experiences of pleasure are valuable only if they contribute to universal happiness
Intrinsic value exists in both mental states and external goods
Experiences are not intrinsically valuable unless they are freely chosen
questions.explain: Ethical Hedonism states that experiences of pleasure are intrinsically good, experiences of pain are intrinsically bad, and they are the only items of intrinsic value with which ethics is concerned.

questions.q: Which of Bentham's felicific calculus dimensions measures how long a pleasure or pain lasts?
options: Intensity
Propinquity
Duration
Fecundity
Purity
questions.explain: Duration measures how long the pleasure or pain lasts. The seven dimensions are: intensity, duration, certainty, propinquity, fecundity, purity, and extent.

questions.q: What logical fallacy does Mill commit in Stage 1 of his proof that happiness is the only intrinsic good?
options: Begging the question
Fallacy of Equivocation: 'desirable' shifts between 'able to be desired' and 'worthy of being desired'
Fallacy of Composition
False dilemma
Argument from authority
questions.explain: Stage 1 commits the Fallacy of Equivocation because Mill slides from the empirical claim that people desire happiness to the normative claim that happiness is worthy of being desired.

questions.q: What is the 'expert judges problem' as an objection to Mill's Qualitative Hedonism?
options: Expert judges are too few in number
Competent judges must have developed capacities to enjoy the pleasures being ranked, but there is no guarantee they will reach universal or near-universal agreement about qualitative rankings
Mill assumes experts exist who have experienced all types of pleasure
The preferences of experts may be biased
Mill provides no clear method for selecting judges
questions.explain: Objection 2 points out that while competent judges must have developed capacities to enjoy the pleasures being ranked, there is no guarantee they will agree.

questions.q: In the Generic Principle of Utility, when is an action A in circumstances C considered right?
options: When the agent believes it is right
When doing A produces as high a utility as would any alternative action the agent could perform
When doing A follows a moral rule accepted by most people
When doing A is intended to maximize overall happiness
When doing A produces utility greater than the agent's own previous actions
questions.explain: The Generic Principle of Utility states that an action A in C is right iff doing A would produce as high a utility as would any alternative action the agent could perform instead.

questions.q: What does the Principle of Hedonistic Utilitarianism (PHU) say about the relationship between pleasure, pain, and right action?
options: Pleasure and pain are equally weighted
An action is right iff it produces at least as high an overall balance of pleasure versus pain as would any other alternative action available to the agent
An action is right only if it maximizes the total quantity of pleasure in the world
An action is right if it increases pleasure for at least one person without causing pain for others
An action is right if the agent believes it will produce more pleasure than pain
questions.explain: PHU states that an action A in C is right iff doing A would produce at least as high an overall balance of pleasure versus pain as would any other alternative action open to the agent.

questions.q: In R. M. Hare's Two Levels of Moral Thought, why is the intuitive level necessary if utilitarianism is true?
options: At the intuitive level, we follow learned moral rules because full utilitarian calculation is not always feasible in ordinary moral life; the intuitive level justifies rule-following while the critical level preserves deliberation for hard cases
The intuitive level represents the general happiness that utilitarianism seeks to maximize
The intuitive level accounts for the fact that people have non-utilitarian moral intuitions that conflict with utilitarianism
The intuitive level is where subjective rightness is determined
The intuitive level provides the basic facts about pleasure and pain upon which calculation depends
questions.explain: Hare argues that ordinary moral life operates at the intuitive level (following rules learned early on) because full utilitarian calculation is infeasible for every decision.

questions.q: What structural questions must any consequentialist theory answer, according to the lecture?
options: Is consequentialism compatible with deontological rules? and Can moral agents calculate utility?
What is the nature of happiness? and How is happiness distributed among individuals?
Which theory of value? (What is intrinsically good?) and How is right action related to value? (Maximise, satisfice, or something else?)
Which moral theory is more fundamental? and What role do intentions play in morality?
How do we determine the intrinsic goods? and Can we measure them scientifically?
questions.explain: Any consequentialist theory must answer: (1) Which theory of value—what things are intrinsically good or bad? (2) How is right action related to value—maximize, satisfice, or something else?

questions.q: According to utilitarian deontic theory, an action is 'optional' when which of the following conditions holds?
options: It is morally irrelevant and may be freely chosen or rejected
It produces utility above the minimum acceptable threshold
It is tied for first place with at least one other action in utility
It benefits the agent without harming others
It aligns with conventional moral rules
questions.explain: An action is optional iff it is tied for first place (equal utility) with at least one other action. Optional actions have equal utility to the best available action, not merely acceptable utility.

questions.q: Why does the gap between Objective Wrong and Subjective Right create a problem for consequentialist theory?
options: It demonstrates that consequentialism ignores the agent's intentions and beliefs
It shows that the actual outcomes may diverge from expected outcomes, making it unclear whether to base rightness on actual or expected utility
It proves that moral agents cannot reliably determine the consequences of their actions
It reveals that utilitarianism is incompatible with moral responsibility
It shows that hedonism cannot account for moral value beyond pleasure
questions.explain: The tension between actual and expected rightness arises because a fully expected-utility action may turn out to be worse in reality while remaining justified given the agent's information.

questions.q: What is the Problem of Ignorance (無知問題) in consequentialism?
options: Moral agents are inherently incapable of calculating utility accurately
To apply the principle of utility in any concrete situation one would need to know the utilities of all available alternatives, which is often infeasible
The principle of utility itself cannot be logically justified or proven
Ignorance about one's own values prevents sincere moral deliberation
People lack knowledge of how their actions affect others' happiness
questions.explain: The Problem of Ignorance presents a practical objection to PHU: applying it would require knowing the utilities of all alternatives, which is typically infeasible.

questions.q: In Derek Parfit's Mine Shafts thought experiment, why does Gate 3 have the highest expected utility?
options: It saves the maximum number of miners if they happen to be in shaft A
It has a 50% chance of saving all 100 miners without risking total failure
It saves 90 miners regardless of which shaft contains the miners, giving an expected utility of 90
It produces the most benefit weighted by the probability of each outcome
It is the only gate that saves some miners in both possible scenarios
questions.explain: Gate 3 saves 90 miners in both scenarios, giving expected utility = (0.5 × 90) + (0.5 × 90) = 90. Gates 1 and 2 each have expected utility = 50.

questions.q: What is the key criterion Mill proposes for determining that one type of pleasure is qualitatively superior to another?
options: The superior pleasure must last longer than inferior pleasures
Consistent preference by competent judges, even at the cost of more discontent, establishes qualitative superiority
The superior pleasure must produce more physical intensity in the body
The superior pleasure must be desired by the majority of people
The superior pleasure must require less effort to achieve
questions.explain: Mill's criterion is that if those who have experienced both types of pleasure consistently prefer one type even knowing it brings more discontent, then that pleasure is qualitatively superior.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes what the Fallacy of Composition in Stage 2 of Mill's Proof claims?
options: The concept of 'general happiness' is logically incoherent if individual happinesses are incommensurable
From the fact that each part has a property, it does not follow that the whole has that property
Mill assumes that if each person desires their happiness, the aggregate must also be desired
Each person's happiness contributes equally to general happiness, so the sum equals the total
Individual desires aggregate to collective desires through simple addition
questions.explain: The Fallacy of Composition in Stage 2 states: from the fact that each part has a property, it does not follow that the whole has that property.

questions.q: What is the primary distinction between the Fallacy of Equivocation in Stage 1 and the Fallacy of Composition in Stage 2 of Mill's Proof?
options: Stage 1 involves mathematical error; Stage 2 involves linguistic confusion
Stage 1 is a semantic slip between descriptive and normative meanings; Stage 2 is a logical leap from individual to collective
Both are semantic errors but apply to different parts of the proof
Stage 1 concerns happiness itself; Stage 2 concerns the nature of desire
Stage 1 is an informal fallacy; Stage 2 is a formal logical fallacy
questions.explain: Stage 1's Fallacy of Equivocation is a semantic error—the word 'desirable' shifts meaning without acknowledgment. Stage 2's Fallacy of Composition is a logical error—assuming a property of parts transfers to the whole without justification.

questions.q: According to Expected Consequences Utilitarianism (ECU), when is an action right?
options: When the action produces the greatest actual utility, regardless of what the agent expected
When the action has as high an expected utility as any alternative action the agent could perform
When the agent reasonably believes the action will maximize utility relative to alternatives
When the action follows rules that, if generally adopted, would maximize expected utility
When the action produces utility equal to the agent's subjective assessment of value
questions.explain: ECU defines rightness in terms of expected utility (probability-weighted sum of outcomes), not actual utility. An action is right iff it has as high expected utility as any alternative.

questions.q: What does the Subjective Principle of Utility (SPU) claim about the relationship between an agent's beliefs and subjective rightness?
options: An action is subjectively right if and only if the agent actually believes it is the best choice
An action is subjectively right if the agent believes it has as high expected utility as any alternative the agent believes is open to her (stated as 'if,' not 'iff')
An action is subjectively right whenever the agent has any reasonable belief that it might be good
An action is subjectively right if the agent's beliefs about expected utility match the objective facts
An action is subjectively right only if the agent's expected utility calculation is mathematically correct
questions.explain: SPU uses 'if,' not 'iff,' meaning it gives a sufficient condition for subjective rightness, not a necessary and sufficient condition.

questions.q: In the context of the Mine Shafts thought experiment, why is Phil's action of closing Gate 3 considered subjectively right even though it might be objectively wrong?
options: Phil's action is subjectively right because it follows a rule that would maximize expected utility if adopted by everyone

Phil believes Gate 3 has the highest expected utility (90) given his information, and acting on the best available subjective judgment makes the action subjectively right, even if the actual outcome is worse
Phil's action is subjectively right because it produces a good outcome for at least some miners
Phil is subjectively right because his intention is to save as many miners as possible
Phil is subjectively right because closing Gate 3 is the average of the utilities of the other gates
questions.explain: Phil's subjective rightness is based on his beliefs about expected utility at the time of decision. Gate 3 has expected utility = 90, higher than Gates 1 and 2 (each = 50).

questions.q: According to the framework presented, how can an action be objectively wrong yet not blameworthy?
options: When the action was taken inadvertently without the agent's full awareness
When the agent is subjectively right—acting on the best available subjective judgment, making the agent not blameworthy despite the worse actual outcome
When the action follows moral rules accepted by the agent's community
When the agent's intentions are good, even though the consequences are bad
When the action produces some benefit to someone, even if not the maximum possible benefit
questions.explain: Blameworthiness is not the same as objective wrongness. Phil can close Gate 3, believe it is best given his information (subjectively right), act conscientiously, yet have it turn out that Gate 1 would have saved more miners (objectively wrong).

questions.q: What is the relationship between the two theses 'value independent of the right' and 'explanatory priority of value' in consequentialism?
options: They are two ways of stating the same idea—that value and rightness are unrelated concepts
Value is independent of the right (it exists prior), and this independence explains why rightness must be derived from value facts rather than the reverse
They represent conflicting claims: independence suggests separation, while priority suggests connection
The first thesis is about metaphysics; the second is about epistemology—how we can know what is right
They together establish that rightness is the more fundamental concept in moral theory
questions.explain: These two theses work together: value exists independently (prior and separate from our concepts of rightness), and this fact gives value explanatory priority—we explain rightness by appeal to value.

questions.q: Which of the following is an objection to Mill's Qualitative Hedonism that relies on a logical dilemma?
options: Mill cannot explain why some pleasures are qualitatively different without abandoning his fundamental commitment to hedonism
Either quality is about the intrinsic nature of mental pleasure states (collapsing to quantitative hedonism) or it is not (forsaking hedonism entirely)
Competent judges will never agree on qualitative rankings because preferences are subjective
Quality cannot be measured or calculated in the way Bentham's calculus measures quantity
Qualitative pleasures are too rare and difficult to achieve for practical moral guidance
questions.explain: Objection 1 presents a dilemma: if quality is about intrinsic nature of mental states, only intensity/duration distinguish them (reducing to quantitative hedonism); if quality is NOT about intrinsic nature, Mill has abandoned hedonism.

questions.q: What is Mill's three-stage proof attempting to establish, and what is the conclusion of Stage 1?
options: The proof attempts to establish that happiness is the only intrinsic good; Stage 1 concludes that each person's happiness is an intrinsic good to that person
The proof attempts to show that pleasure is the only source of value; Stage 1 concludes that desire is a reliable indicator of value
The proof attempts to demonstrate that utility can be calculated; Stage 1 concludes that utility is proportional to pleasure
The proof attempts to justify the Principle of Hedonistic Utilitarianism; Stage 1 concludes that all people share common values
The proof attempts to reconcile hedonism with virtue; Stage 1 concludes that virtue produces the greatest pleasure
questions.explain: Mill's three-stage proof aims to establish that happiness is the sole intrinsic good. Stage 1 concludes that each person's happiness is an intrinsic good to that person.

questions.q: Which of the following best explains why the Problem of Ignorance motivates a distinction between moral criteria and decision procedures?
options: Agents cannot know their own values, so they must rely on general rules and social conventions instead
The principle of utility can be a criterion for what makes an action right without being a practical procedure agents can always follow due to ignorance of utilities
Moral criteria are objective, while decision procedures are subjective and based on individual beliefs
Decision procedures require certainty, while moral criteria allow for probability and uncertainty
Moral criteria apply universally, while decision procedures vary among different agents
questions.explain: The Problem of Ignorance (infeasibility of knowing all utilities) does not refute consequentialism if we separate the criterion for rightness (actual consequences) from the decision procedure (expected consequences given available information).

questions.q: What does it mean to say that in utilitarian theory, 'personal value alone' is relevant according to the third thesis of consequentialism?
options: Only the personal preferences of individual agents matter; collective values are irrelevant
Only the value that accrues to individuals (persons, sentient beings) counts when assessing outcomes; the value intrinsic to objects or abstract entities does not count morally
Each person's value judgments are equally valid and cannot be compared or ranked
Personal values are more important than social or collective goods in moral reasoning
The value of an outcome depends entirely on how each individual person subjectively experiences it
questions.explain: The third thesis states that only the value accruing to individuals (persons, sentient beings) counts—not the intrinsic value of objects, institutions, or abstract ideals.

questions.q: How do the four components of Classical Act Utilitarianism (maximising, welfarism, universalism, and impartialism) work together to define right action?
options: Maximising is the goal; welfarism is the method; universalism is the scope; impartialism is the distribution principle
All four components work together, but impartialism and universalism are logically redundant because both require considering everyone

Maximising specifies that right action produces the greatest total welfare; welfarism specifies that welfare is the value to maximize; universalism ensures all affected individuals count; impartialism ensures each counts equally
These components allow individual agents to pursue their own happiness while contributing to collective well-being
Together they establish that an action is right iff it maximizes the total welfare of all equally-weighted individuals affected by it
questions.explain: The four components define right action by specifying: (1) what to do (maximize), (2) what to maximize (welfare), (3) whose welfare counts (all affected), (4) how much each counts (equally).

questions.q: What is the relationship between Blameless Wrongdoing and the SPU (Subjective Principle of Utility)?
options: SPU is a criterion for blameworthiness, so any action satisfying SPU is automatically both subjectively and objectively right
An agent whose action satisfies SPU (subjectively right) is not blameworthy even if the action is objectively wrong because blameworthiness tracks subjective, not objective, rightness
Blameless wrongdoing occurs when an agent violates SPU by having irrational beliefs about expected utility
An agent's action can be subjectively right (satisfying SPU) and yet objectively wrong, making the agent blameworthy in the objective sense but not blameworthiness-wise
SPU explains why some objectively wrong actions are still praiseworthy if the agent's intentions are good
questions.explain: When an agent acts on the best available subjective judgment (satisfying SPU), the action is subjectively right. Even if it turns out to be objectively wrong, the agent is not blameworthy.

questions.q: In consequentialist theory, what significance does the distinction between 'moral criteria' and 'decision procedures' have for resolving the Problem of Ignorance?
options: It eliminates the need for agents to consider consequences when making decisions
It shows that the principle of utility fails as a moral theory because it cannot guide practical action
It allows the principle of utility to remain a valid criterion for rightness even when agents cannot always know all utilities, by using expected utility as a decision procedure
It proves that moral rules are more important than maximizing utility
It demonstrates that subjective rightness is more important than objective rightness
questions.explain: The distinction separates the criterion for what makes an action right (principle of utility) from the procedure for deciding what to do (expected utility calculation given available information). This allows consequentialism to remain true even when perfect knowledge is infeasible.

questions.q: According to the lecture's framework, in what sense can the two-level approach to moral thought preserve utilitarian commitments while acknowledging practical constraints on moral deliberation?
options: By establishing that rules are ultimately what matter morally, not consequences
By showing that some moral decisions do not require consequentialist reasoning at all
By justifying rule-following at the intuitive level (where utility calculation is infeasible) while preserving full utilitarian deliberation at the critical level (where novel conflicts arise)
By demonstrating that agents are never required to perform utilitarian calculations in practice
By proving that intuitive moral rules always maximize expected utility
questions.explain: Hare's two-level approach reconciles utilitarian theory with practical limitations: ordinary moral life follows learned rules without calculation (intuitive level), but when rules conflict or novel situations arise, agents engage in full deliberate utilitarian reasoning (critical level). This preserves both the theoretical claim that consequences determine rightness and the practical reality that we cannot always calculate.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the standard method for critiquing consequentialism?
options: Constructing cases where the theory's verdict clashes with moral intuitions
Analyzing the logical consistency of utilitarian premises
Comparing consequentialism with ancient virtue ethics
Identifying empirical errors in utility calculations
Examining the linguistic meaning of consequentialist terms
questions.explain: The lecture explicitly states that the standard method of critique is to construct cases where the theory's verdict is at odds with considered moral beliefs. Logical consistency and linguistic analysis are separate from the intuition-clash methodology.

questions.q: What is the key issue raised by the retributive justice objection to utilitarianism?
options: Utilitarianism can require punishing innocent people if it maximizes utility
Utilitarianism fails to distribute utility equally among rich and poor
Utilitarianism overvalues the suffering of criminals compared to law-abiding citizens
Utilitarianism ignores the importance of rehabilitation in the justice system
Utilitarianism treats all moral agents as having equal culpability
questions.explain: The framing case shows that utilitarianism appears to entail that a police chief should frame an innocent, socially isolated person if it maximizes utility by preventing riots. This directly conflicts with the intuition that punishing the innocent is always wrong, regardless of consequences.

questions.q: In the medical sacrifice case, what is the primary objection to the utilitarian verdict?
options: The surgeon would violate the Hippocratic Oath, which explicitly forbids harvesting organs
Utilitarianism requires sacrificing one patient to save three, which conflicts with the prohibition on killing the innocent
The patient's family would sue the hospital for malpractice if they discovered the truth
Modern medical technology makes it impossible to hide such an action from the public
The utilitarian calculation would be impossible without perfect knowledge of utility values
questions.explain: The case shows utilitarianism appears to require sacrificing one innocent patient to save three others. The Lazari-Radek and Singer variant shows that even if the action could be hidden (no discovery of foul play), consequentialism still seems to endorse it, clashing with the intuition that killing one innocent person is never permissible.

questions.q: Classical utilitarianism has three structural features. Which is characterized as the requirement that actions produce the highest net value compared to alternatives?
options: Impartiality
Maximization
Directness
Aggregation
Neutrality
questions.explain: Maximization is defined as the requirement that rightness/wrongness depends on producing the highest net value compared to alternatives. Impartiality concerns equal weighting of consequences for all parties; directness concerns how actions are evaluated based on associated utility.

questions.q: The distributive justice objection targets which structural feature of classical utilitarianism?
options: Directness — it fails to account for how actions affect distribution
Maximization — it permits unequal outcomes as long as aggregate utility is highest
Impartiality — it gives equal weight to all persons regardless of need
Neutrality — it does not assign special weight to fairness
Aggregation — it sums utility without considering the well-being of individuals
questions.explain: Utilitarianism's indifference to how utility is distributed across persons (maximizing aggregate without concern for equality) is the core issue. Utilitarianism prefers a scheme with higher total utility even if most people are below the poverty line, because equal distribution as such carries no intrinsic weight.

questions.q: Why does the promising case present a conflict for consequentialism?
options: Promises made to terminally ill people are less binding than promises to healthy people
Consequentialist calculation would recommend breaking the promise if circumstances change and the promise-breaker gains more utility
The executor of the estate has superior knowledge about the daughter's financial situation
Promise-keeping obligations are enforced only by legal contracts, not moral commitments
The daughter's lottery winnings eliminate the original reason for the promise
questions.explain: By age 21, the daughter no longer needs the money while the agent's circumstances have deteriorated, so consequential calculation appears to require breaking the promise. This clashes with the moral force of the original commitment, suggesting that the binding force of promises cannot be fully captured by utility considerations.

questions.q: The demandingness objection claims that utilitarianism leaves no legitimate space for which of the following?
options: Moral disagreement with strangers
Personal projects and preferences
Punishment of wrongdoers
Redistribution of wealth
Correction of past injustices
questions.explain: The demandingness objection argues that the impartialist standpoint of utilitarianism requires always maximizing utility, leaving no room for personal projects like gardening when volunteering would produce greater overall benefit. The gardening case illustrates how personal interests are constantly overridden by utilitarian calculation.

questions.q: What distinguishes the special obligations objection from the demandingness objection?
options: Special obligations concern the amount of sacrifice required; demandingness concerns whether partiality is permissible
Demandingness concerns the amount of sacrifice required; special obligations concern whether partiality toward loved ones is permissible
Special obligations apply only to close family relationships; demandingness applies to all moral agents
Special obligations are based on legal contracts; demandingness is based on moral intuitions
Demandingness objections target rule consequentialism; special obligations objections target act consequentialism
questions.explain: The lecture explicitly states this distinction: demandingness concerns how much sacrifice is required overall, while special obligations concerns whether partiality toward loved ones (like spending money on one's own child rather than a more academically promising neighbor) is ever permissible. These are distinct issues.

questions.q: Consequentialists have adopted three broad strategies for responding to objections. Which one involves rejecting one or more of the structural features (directness, maximization, impartiality)?
options: Rebutting the objections directly
Defending an alternative theory of welfare
Structural modification
Changing the definition of utility
Appealing to moral intuitions
questions.explain: The three broad strategies are: (1) rebutting objections directly, (2) defending alternative welfare theories, and (3) rejecting one or more structural features. Structural modification covers responses like satisficing (rejecting maximization) and rule consequentialism (modifying how evaluation is applied).

questions.q: According to the bold denial response, what should consequentialists do when faced with counterintuitive verdicts?
options: Acknowledge that classical consequentialism is false and adopt a different ethical theory
Challenge the authority of moral intuitions and reject the counterintuitive intuition
Claim that the thought experiment fails to accurately represent real-world scenarios
Distinguish between intuitions about rules and intuitions about individual acts
Modify the theory to make more room for special obligations
questions.explain: Bold denial accepts the counterintuitive verdict and challenges the reliability of moral intuitions. Joshua Greene's quote emphasizes that intuitions are post-hoc rationalizations and products of evolution or cultural conditioning, not reliable guides to moral truth. The strategy is to reject the intuition, not the theory.

questions.q: What is a key limitation of the remote effects response to objection cases?
options: It works best for medical ethics cases but fails in political philosophy
It does not work when cases are carefully stipulated to exclude long-term and social consequences
It requires knowledge of future events that we cannot possibly possess
It assumes that public trust is more valuable than individual welfare
It applies only to cases involving dishonest action
questions.explain: The remote effects response argues that stipulating consequences is unrealistic in cases like the framing case or medical sacrifice case. However, the limitation is explicit: when thought experiments are carefully designed to exclude social and long-term consequences (e.g., no risk of exposure, no erosion of public trust), the remote effects response does not work, and bold denial is needed instead.

questions.q: How does satisficing consequentialism differ from classical act consequentialism?
options: It replaces the maximization requirement with a threshold requirement
It evaluates rules instead of individual actions
It incorporates a richer account of human welfare
It gives greater weight to the interests of the worst-off
It prioritizes the actual consequences over the intended consequences
questions.explain: Satisficing consequentialism (SC) formula: Action A is right iff its consequences are 'good enough' and meet or exceed a specified threshold, even if some alternative would produce even better consequences. This replaces the maximizing requirement of classical consequentialism with a more permissive threshold standard.

questions.q: What do the charity theft case and the rescue case demonstrate about satisficing consequentialism?
options: Satisficing consequentialism allows too little moral discretion
Satisficing consequentialism is too permissive: it permits clearly wrong acts whenever they meet the threshold
Satisficing consequentialism requires impossible calculations of utility
Satisficing consequentialism fails to account for special obligations
Satisficing consequentialism demands excessive sacrifice from moral agents
questions.explain: The charity theft case (agent keeps donations when giving them all would exceed threshold) and rescue case (pilot saves 2 campers when 6 could be saved) both show SC allows clearly wrong acts as long as utility exceeds the threshold. This demonstrates SC is too permissive, not a resolution of the demandingness problem.

questions.q: According to rule consequentialism, what determines whether an action is right or wrong?
options: Whether the action itself produces the highest net value
Whether the action is required or prohibited by an ideal code of rules selected by acceptance utility
Whether the action satisfies a threshold utility requirement
Whether the action accords with common moral intuitions
Whether the action respects the rights and interests of others
questions.explain: The RC formula states: Action A is right iff A is not prohibited by an ideal code of rules. The ideal code is the set of rules whose acceptance utility (value of accepting those rules) would be at least as great as any alternative code. This is fundamentally different from act consequentialism's focus on individual action consequences.

questions.q: How does rule consequentialism respond to the medical sacrifice objection?
options: It denies that sacrificing one patient can ever be justified
A rule permitting physicians to sacrifice innocent patients would have lower acceptance utility than a rule prohibiting it
It shows that the medical sacrifice case involves a failure of remote effects reasoning
It argues that the intuition against sacrificing patients is merely cultural conditioning
It permits the sacrifice only if the patient has consented in advance
questions.explain: RC can respond that a rule permitting sacrifice of innocent patients would undermine trust in the medical profession and produce lower overall acceptance utility than a rule prohibiting such sacrifice. Rules prohibiting harm to innocent patients would have higher acceptance utility than permissive rules.

questions.q: What is the collapse objection to rule consequentialism?
options: Rule consequentialism collapses into virtue ethics when taken to its logical conclusion
Iterating to ever-more-complex rules eventually reproduces act consequentialism (R4 becomes extensionally equivalent to AC)
Rule consequentialism is unable to explain why any rules have moral force
Rule consequentialism requires impossible knowledge about the consequences of adopting rules
Rule consequentialism fails because rules are too abstract to apply to concrete cases
questions.explain: The collapse objection shows that as we iterate to more complex rules (R1 → R3 → R4) to handle edge cases, R4 eventually becomes 'Keep promises unless some alternative produces greater value.' This rule is extensionally equivalent to act consequentialism—they agree on every action's rightness/wrongness—so RC ultimately collapses into AC.

questions.q: What does extensionally equivalent mean in the context of the rule consequentialism collapse objection?
options: Two theories extend the same moral concepts to all human beings
Two theories use the same mathematical formulas to calculate utility
Two theories agree on which actions are right/wrong in every possible case
Two theories apply their reasoning in the same sequence of logical steps
Two theories give equal weight to the same set of moral considerations
questions.explain: The lecture defines extensionally equivalent as meaning the two theories agree on the deontic status (right/wrong) of every action. R4 and act consequentialism produce identical verdicts in all cases, even though R4 is formulated as a rule while AC evaluates acts directly. This shows the formulation difference is merely superficial.

questions.q: What is the primary challenge raised by Nozick's experience machine to hedonistic utilitarianism?
options: It shows that pleasure is easier to measure than philosophers had believed
It demonstrates that subjective experience alone is not sufficient for a good life
It proves that happiness is the only intrinsic good
It reveals that people consistently make poor decisions about their own welfare
It shows that external reality does not affect personal well-being
questions.explain: Most people would refuse to plug into the experience machine permanently, suggesting that actual achievement, real relationships, and contact with reality matter beyond mere felt experience. This challenges hedonism's assumption that only subjective states have intrinsic value, suggesting objective accomplishment also has independent worth.

questions.q: Which of the following is a problem for desire fulfilment consequentialism as a theory of welfare?
options: It assigns excessive importance to happiness and pleasure
Not all fulfilled desires contribute to the agent's welfare; moreover, fulfilment of horrendous desires has no intrinsic value
It fails to account for the role of justice in human flourishing
It makes welfare calculations too complex for practical moral reasoning
It assumes that desires are always rationally formed and informed
questions.explain: The lecture identifies two problems: (1) Not all desire fulfilments benefit the agent (e.g., a desire satisfied without the agent's knowledge); (2) Fulfilment of horrendous desires does not seem to have intrinsic value. These suggest desire fulfilment alone is not a sufficient account of welfare.

questions.q: What is the distinguishing feature of perfectionist consequentialism's account of value?
options: It holds that pleasure and happiness are the only intrinsic goods
It defines the good by objective standards of human flourishing and certain excellences
It prioritizes the satisfaction of informed rational desires
It bases value judgments entirely on empirical preferences
It rejects the possibility of objective standards in ethics
questions.explain: Perfectionist consequentialism holds that certain excellences—artistic, intellectual, moral—have intrinsic value independent of whether they produce pleasure or fulfil desires. This non-welfarist version defines the good by objective standards of human flourishing, making it closer to natural law theory in its account of value.

questions.q: According to the lecture, why is the 'directness' feature of classical utilitarianism often misunderstood?
options: Students confuse 'direct' evaluation with evaluation based only on immediate consequences
The term 'direct' is never used consistently in philosophical literature
Directness is actually not a real feature of utilitarian theory
Classical utilitarians themselves disagreed about what directness means
Directness has no practical implications for evaluating actions
questions.explain: The exam trap explicitly warns that 'direct' refers to how actions are evaluated (based on associated utility), not whether consequences are immediate. Remote consequences still count under classical utilitarianism. Students often confuse 'direct' with 'immediate,' which is a critical error.

questions.q: What does the threshold in satisficing consequentialism serve to accomplish?
options: It identifies which consequences are morally significant and which are not
It eliminates the demandingness problem by permitting 'good enough' consequences even if better alternatives exist
It ensures equal distribution of utility among all affected parties
It provides an objective measure of what counts as a desirable outcome
It prevents agents from making calculation errors in complex scenarios
questions.explain: The threshold is designed to relieve excessive demandingness by permitting an agent to stop optimizing once an action meets or exceeds a specified threshold utility. This allows gardening on Sunday even if volunteering would produce higher utility, provided gardening's consequences exceed the threshold. However, SC's permissiveness creates new problems.

questions.q: How does the concept of acceptance utility function in rule consequentialism?
options: It measures the total amount of pleasure that would result from accepting a rule
It calculates the value of the consequences associated with accepting a code of rules
It determines which agents are required to follow a particular rule
It quantifies the amount of moral effort required to comply with a rule
It assesses whether a rule conflicts with other established moral principles
questions.explain: The ideal code in RC is the set of rules whose acceptance utility (the value of the consequences of accepting and following those rules) would be at least as great as any alternative code. Rules are evaluated not by their immediate action-consequences, but by the overall value of living under that code of rules.

questions.q: Why might desire fulfilment consequentialism appeal to philosophers dissatisfied with hedonistic utilitarianism?
options: Because it permits agents to pursue their own projects without restriction
Because it replaces the subjective experience-based account of welfare with fulfillment of desires, which seems more objective
Because it avoids the problem of calculating pleasure and pain
Because it aligns more closely with Rawlsian principles of justice
Because it requires less knowledge about other people's mental states
questions.explain: Philosophers dissatisfied with hedonism (which grounds welfare only in subjective pleasure) might prefer desire fulfilment as a more objective and agent-centered account of welfare. However, the lecture shows this approach faces its own problems regarding which desires count and how to treat horrendous desires.

questions.q: Which response strategy available to consequentialists directly challenges the reliability of moral intuitions themselves?
options: Remote effects response
Structural modification response
Bold denial response
Alternative welfare theory response
Collapse objection response
questions.explain: Bold denial (not remote effects or structural modification) challenges the authority of the moral intuitions themselves, treating them as post-hoc rationalizations rather than reliable guides to truth. Greene's argument exemplifies this: feelings may be products of evolution or culture, not genuine moral insight.

questions.q: What is the significance of the education case in illustrating the special obligations objection?
options: It shows that consequentialism wrongly prioritizes utility over love between family members
It demonstrates that if the neighbor's child would produce better consequences, consequentialism requires funding the neighbor rather than one's own child
It proves that parental obligations are based on genetics rather than moral principles
It reveals that educational opportunity is more valuable than other forms of utility
It suggests that special obligations cannot be reconciled with any form of ethical theory
questions.explain: The education case shows that utilitarianism's impartiality would require funding the more academically promising neighbor's child rather than one's own son, if consequences would be better. This clashes with the intuition that there is moral weight to special parental obligations to one's own children, independent of comparative consequences.

questions.q: Which of the following best captures why the promising case presents a distinctive challenge that the remote effects response cannot fully address?
options: It involves highly personal and subjective emotional attachments
If the case is stipulated so that breaking the promise causes no external harm or loss of trust, remote effects reasoning does not explain why promise-breaking remains wrong
The person making the promise was terminally ill and could not anticipate future circumstances
Modern legal systems no longer recognize promises made to deceased persons
The daughter's financial independence eliminates all moral weight from the original promise
questions.explain: The promising case challenges remote effects reasoning because even if we stipulate that breaking the promise causes no erosion of trust, no exposure, or other negative social effects, the agent's obligation to keep the promise seems to remain. This suggests that remote effects cannot be the full explanation of why promise-breaking is wrong.

questions.q: The framing case and the medical sacrifice case are both designed to illustrate conflicts with which type of moral intuition?
options: Intuitions about demandingness and sacrifice
Intuitions about justice and rights
Intuitions about partiality and special relationships
Intuitions about human flourishing and excellences
Intuitions about the limits of moral duty
questions.explain: Both cases are presented as examples of clashes with intuitions about justice and rights. The framing case shows utilitarian permission to punish the innocent; the medical sacrifice case shows utilitarian permission to kill an innocent. These clash with the strong intuition that certain acts (like punishing the innocent) are fundamentally unjust.

questions.q: Which of the following best explains why perfectionist consequentialism bears resemblance to Aquinas's natural law theory?
options: Both theories reject consequentialist evaluation of actions
Both theories evaluate actions based on rules rather than outcomes
Both theories define the good by objective excellences and human flourishing rather than subjective states
Both theories prioritize divine command as the source of moral truth
Both theories reject the distinction between moral and non-moral values
questions.explain: The resemblance lies in the theory of value: perfectionist consequentialism, like Aquinas's natural law theory, appeals to objective standards of human flourishing and excellence. However, perfectionist consequentialism retains the consequentialist structure of evaluating actions by outcomes, unlike deontological natural law theory. The link is about value, not ethical framework.

questions.q: How does the gardening case illustrate the core concern of the demandingness objection?
options: It shows that personal activities are never morally justified unless they maximize utility
It demonstrates that spending time on personal projects (like gardening) is permitted only by rule consequentialism
It illustrates that utilitarianism's impartial standpoint leaves no room for personal projects when volunteering would produce greater overall benefit
It proves that hedonic pleasures are less valuable than altruistic sacrifices
It suggests that consequentialism is fundamentally incompatible with human psychology
questions.explain: The gardening case shows the agent pulled between personal interest (gardening) and the impartial utilitarian obligation to volunteer for greater benefit. The concern is that utilitarianism seems to always require the option with highest aggregate utility, leaving no legitimate space for personal projects—a result many find unreasonable.

questions.q: Which of the following best defines Ethical Egoism?
options: An action is right if it produces the greatest happiness for the greatest number
An action is right if it affects the self-interest of the person acting in a positive way
An action is right if it conforms to universal moral laws
An action is right if it is performed with good intentions
An action is right if it benefits the majority of stakeholders
questions.explain: EE is an agent-centered theory: rightness depends on how an action affects the self-interest of the actor. The first option describes Utilitarianism, not EE. The third and fourth describe deontological or virtue approaches.

questions.q: According to the formal theory of right conduct in Ethical Egoism, when is an action obligatory?
options: When it produces the greatest pleasure
When following it causes no harm to others
When the agent's performing it would produce higher agent utility than any other action available
When the agent intends to benefit themselves
When society approves of the action
questions.explain: An action is obligatory in EE iff performing it would produce higher agent utility than any alternative. Option 1 could be Hedonism; option 4 is too vague about intention vs outcome.

questions.q: What is the key difference between the EE definition of 'right' and the definition of 'optional action'?
options: Right actions must be obligatory; optional actions may be permissible
Optional actions require a tie with at least one alternative that produces equal utility; the right-action definition sets a threshold without requiring a tie
Right actions always benefit society; optional actions only benefit the agent
Optional actions are chosen freely; right actions are chosen by necessity
Right actions maximize utility; optional actions minimize harm
questions.explain: The exam trap is recognizing that while the definitions sound similar, optional actions require at least one alternative at the same utility level. The EE right-action definition simply describes what counts as right without requiring a tie condition.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a property of Ethical Egoism as described in the lecture?
options: Consequentialist
Agent-Relative
Impartialist
Maximizing
Prudentialist
questions.explain: EE is agent-relative or agent-centered: only the actor's own welfare counts. It is not impartialist — impartialism would treat all parties' interests equally, the opposite of EE's focus on self-interest.

questions.q: What distinguishes Objectivist EE from Subjectivist EE?
options: Objectivist EE applies only to individuals; Subjectivist EE applies to groups
Objectivist EE bases rightness on actual agent utility maximization; Subjectivist EE bases it on the agent's belief about utility
Objectivist EE requires empirical verification; Subjectivist EE does not
Objectivist EE is rational; Subjectivist EE is irrational
Objectivist EE values long-term utility; Subjectivist EE values short-term utility
questions.explain: The key distinction is fact vs belief. Under Objectivist EE, an action is right if it actually maximizes utility. Under Subjectivist EE, it is right if the agent believes it does. Subjectivism makes rightness dependent on the agent's epistemic state.
