questions.q: According to the lecture, how do Ethical Egoism and Rational Egoism differ?
options: EE is about morality; RE is about rationality
EE requires maximization; RE permits any satisficing level
EE is empirically testable; RE is not
EE applies only to individuals; RE applies to groups
EE is older than RE
questions.explain: Both use the same self-interest criterion but apply it to different domains. EE asks 'what makes an action right or wrong?' while RE asks 'what makes an action rational or irrational?' They are 'cousins' sharing a criterion but occupying different normative spaces.

questions.q: What is the fundamental claim of Psychological Egoism?
options: All humans are morally obligated to pursue their self-interest
All humans can be motivated by reasons beyond self-interest
Every deliberate human action is ultimately motivated by the agent's self-interest
Humans are naturally altruistic and must be taught to be selfish
Self-interest and altruism are equally common human motivations
questions.explain: PE is a descriptive claim about human motivation, not a normative claim about what ought to be. It says all deliberate action has self-interest as the ultimate motive, even if intermediate goals appear altruistic.

questions.q: Which of the following is true about Psychological Egoism according to the lecture?
options: It claims people are always consciously aware of their self-interested motives
It restricts ultimate motives to pleasure alone
It includes reflex actions and compulsions as evidence for PE
It allows that people can hold false beliefs about what promotes their self-interest
It denies that intermediate goals can appear altruistic
questions.explain: PE is explicit that people can have false beliefs about their self-interest while still acting from ultimate self-interested motives. It does not require conscious awareness and allows intermediate goals to appear altruistic while the ultimate motive is self-interest.

questions.q: How does Psychological Egoism differ from Psychological Hedonism?
options: Egoism is descriptive; Hedonism is normative
Egoism allows ultimate motives beyond pleasure; Hedonism restricts the ultimate motive to pleasure
Egoism applies to groups; Hedonism applies only to individuals
Egoism is empirically testable; Hedonism is not
Egoism denies conscious calculation; Hedonism requires it
questions.explain: Both are descriptive theories of motivation, but PE is broader: it says any self-interested motive (power, reputation, dominance) drives action. Psychological Hedonism narrows this to pleasure alone.

questions.q: What is Psychological Altruism, and how does it relate to Psychological Egoism?
options: It is a normative theory about how we ought to act; it is opposed to PE
It is a descriptive claim that humans can and sometimes act from the ultimate motive of benefiting others; it opposes PE
It is a claim about rationality; it is complementary to PE
It is the view that altruistic acts are really disguised self-interest; it supports PE
It is a historical position no longer defended; it is incompatible with PE
questions.explain: PA is PE's descriptive opponent: while PE says all ultimate motives are self-interested, PA allows that humans can have ultimate motives of benefiting others. Both are empirical, scientific claims about human motivation.

questions.q: What is the 'ought implies can' principle, and how is it used in the PE-to-EE argument?
options: It states that if you can do something, you ought to do it
It bridges descriptive and normative claims: if one is morally obligated to perform an action, one must be able to perform it
It proves that Psychological Egoism is false
It shows that Ethical Egoism is based on empirical facts about motivation
It establishes that all moral obligations are rational
questions.explain: The principle connects possibility to obligation: one cannot be obligated to do what is impossible. The argument uses it to link PE (what we are capable of doing) to the structure of moral obligation.

questions.q: Which step in the PE-to-EE argument is identified in the lecture as problematic?
options: Step 1: the 'ought implies can' principle
Step 2: the claim that psychological capability entails self-interested motivation
Step 3: the inference from premises 1 and 2
Step 6: the claim that being ultimately motivated by self-interest means maximizing self-interest
Step 7: the conclusion that EE follows from the premises
questions.explain: The lecture flags this as an exam trap: Step 6 assumes that if an action is ultimately motivated by self-interest, then it must maximize the agent's self-interest. This is a logical gap — being motivated by self-interest does not automatically mean the outcome maximizes it.

questions.q: According to the lecture, what is the main finding of Batson's experiments?
options: Participants helped others primarily to reduce their own distress
Participants consistently chose easy escape over helping when possible
Participants helped even when they could easily escape the aversive observation without helping
Participants only helped when they expected social reward
Participants helped less in difficult-escape conditions than easy-escape conditions
questions.explain: Batson predicted that egoism would lead participants to avoid helping when easy escape was available. The finding contradicted this prediction: participants helped even with easy escape, suggesting altruistic rather than purely egoistic motivation.

questions.q: According to the pro-egoistic explanations for helping behavior, why might a person help someone in distress?
options: To genuinely benefit the other person out of altruism
To maximize utility for everyone involved
To reduce the helper's own discomfort through aversive-empathic arousal reduction
To follow universal moral laws about compassion
To satisfy a desire for fairness and impartiality
questions.explain: The pro-egoistic view reinterprets helping as self-interested: the helper is motivated by relieving their own distress at witnessing suffering, not by genuine concern for the other person. This fits PE by recasting apparent altruism as self-interest.

questions.q: What is the 'What You Most Want' Argument, and what is its main premise?
options: An argument that EE is incoherent because agents cannot always maximize utility
An argument that whenever anyone acts, they necessarily do whatever they most want to do
An argument that self-interest and altruism are equally fundamental human motives
An argument that rationality requires acting on conscious desires
An argument that PE cannot be empirically tested
questions.explain: The argument's first premise claims that action always reflects what one 'most wants.' The lecture identifies a rebuttal: 'want' is ambiguous between liking (felt attraction) and explanation (desire doing explanatory work), and under both senses the premise fails.

questions.q: How can the first premise of the 'What You Most Want' Argument be rebutted?
options: By showing that people sometimes lack preferences
By demonstrating that most people are altruistic
By showing that 'want' is ambiguous: under 'liking' sense, people act against their strongest felt attraction; under 'explanatory' sense, the desire doing the explaining need not be self-interested
By proving that consciousness always accompanies action
By showing that rationality overrides desire
questions.explain: The rebuttal exploits the ambiguity in 'want.' If 'want' means what one feels most attracted to, it is false that we always act on that. If 'want' means what explains behavior, the desire explaining an action need not be self-interested.

questions.q: What does the Satisfaction Argument attempt to establish?
options: That ethical egoism is incoherent
That desire-fulfillment always produces pleasure
That whenever one acts, one's ultimate motive is the pleasure or relief from satisfying one's desire — therefore PE is true
That satisfaction is impossible to define objectively
That altruism cannot lead to satisfaction
questions.explain: The Satisfaction Argument links having a desire fulfilled (satisfaction) to feeling pleasure or relief, then infers that this implies self-interested motivation. It derives PE from the phenomenology of desire-fulfillment.

questions.q: How does the Pleasure Argument differ from the Satisfaction Argument?
options: The Pleasure Argument is empirical; the Satisfaction Argument is not
The Satisfaction Argument infers self-interest from desire-fulfillment phenomenology; the Pleasure Argument asserts a deeper metaphysical claim that all desire is fundamentally pleasure-seeking
The Pleasure Argument only applies to desires; the Satisfaction Argument applies to all motives
The Satisfaction Argument is more recent than the Pleasure Argument
They are identical and the lecture uses them interchangeably
questions.explain: The lecture explicitly flags these as distinct. Satisfaction focuses on the psychological fact that desire-fulfillment feels good. Pleasure commits to a metaphysical claim that all desire is fundamentally about maximizing one's own pleasure.

questions.q: According to the lecture, what is the consistency problem for Ethical Egoism?
options: EE cannot explain why we have desires
EE conflicts with the Principle of Non-Interference, which states it is wrong to interfere with someone else's duty
EE is inconsistent with all forms of altruism
EE cannot account for moral obligations
EE requires an impossible calculus of utility
questions.explain: If everyone's duty is to maximize their own self-interest, and duties can conflict, then EE seems to permit interference with others' duty-performance. The Principle of Non-Interference (PNI) and EE appear incompatible.

questions.q: What are the two resolution options for the consistency problem between EE and the Principle of Non-Interference?
options: Reject both EE and PNI entirely
Reject PNI outright, or qualify it to subordinate it to self-interest considerations
Abandon the concept of duty altogether
Adopt a form of utilitarianism instead of EE
Restrict EE to apply only to private actions
questions.explain: One option is to reject PNI as a fundamental moral principle. Another is to reword PNI to say interference is wrong only if it harms your self-interest — making PNI subject to EE's self-interest criterion.

questions.q: What determinacy problem does EE face, and how might it be resolved?
options: We cannot know all consequences, so we cannot apply EE; resolve by using expected agent utility and distinguishing critical vs intuitive moral reasoning
We cannot define self-interest clearly; resolve by adopting objective definitions
Duties cannot be determined from agent utility; resolve by adding other criteria
EE is too simple; resolve by making it more complex
Moral terms are ambiguous; resolve by stipulating new definitions
questions.explain: Like Utilitarianism, EE faces a practical problem: we lack complete information about all effects. EE can adopt expected agent utility (decision-making under uncertainty) and critical vs intuitive reasoning to address this.

questions.q: According to the lecture, what does external support for a moral theory mean?
options: The theory is supported by international consensus
The theory is consistent with, and ideally supported by, well-established theories and assumptions from other fields
The theory is based on divine command
The theory requires support from an external authority
The theory is supported by empirical observation of all people
questions.explain: External support refers to the theory's coherence with other well-established disciplines like psychology, biology, or economics. It addresses whether a normative theory fits with empirical and theoretical knowledge.

questions.q: Do Batson's experimental findings refute Ethical Egoism?
options: Yes, they show that EE is false
No, because EE is a normative theory about obligation, not a descriptive claim about actual motivation
Yes, but only Objectivist EE, not Subjectivist EE
No, but they support Psychological Altruism over Psychological Egoism
Partially, because they suggest EE is unrealistic
questions.explain: This is a crucial distinction. Batson's findings refute PE or the aversive-arousal hypothesis, but they do NOT refute EE. EE is normative (what one ought to do), not descriptive (what people actually do). Empirical facts about motivation do not straightforwardly determine facts about moral obligation.

questions.q: What is the normative/descriptive distinction, and why is it important for EE?
options: Normative theories are true; descriptive theories are false
Normative theories prescribe what ought to be; descriptive theories describe what is. EE is insulated from empirical psychology because facts about motivation do not determine facts about obligation
Normative and descriptive statements are unrelated
Descriptive statements are more important than normative ones
EE is both normative and descriptive
questions.explain: This distinction is central to the lecture's response to empirical objections. Even if PE is false (people are not purely self-interested), it does not follow that EE is false (people are not obligated to maximize self-interest). The domains are separate.

questions.q: Which of the following best captures the relationship between PE and EE according to the lecture?
options: PE entails EE; if PE is true, EE must be true
EE entails PE; if EE is true, all people must be purely self-interested
PE and EE are in different domains (descriptive vs normative); PE might be false while EE remains a legitimate normative position
PE and EE are contradictory; only one can be true
PE and EE are identical; the lecture treats them as the same theory
questions.explain: The PE-to-EE argument tries to derive a normative conclusion from a descriptive premise, but the attempt contains gaps. Even if PE is false, EE can still be a coherent normative theory about what one ought to do.

questions.q: In the context of the PE-to-EE argument, what role does step 4 ('there are actions one is morally obligated to perform') play?
options: It proves that PE is true
It establishes that morality is objective
It triggers the application of 'ought implies can' to derive that obligatory actions must be those one can perform
It contradicts EE
It is an assumption that can be rejected
questions.explain: Step 4 is a necessary premise: if there are any moral obligations, then by 'ought implies can,' those actions must be psychologically performable, and therefore (by PE) ultimately motivated by self-interest. Rejecting step 4 breaks the chain.

questions.q: According to the lecture, what is aversive-empathic arousal reduction as a pro-egoistic explanation?
options: A form of altruism where one helps to benefit others
A theory that helping is motivated by reducing the helper's own discomfort at witnessing suffering
A claim that empathy is rational
A theory that all emotions are self-interested
A form of psychological hedonism
questions.explain: Aversive-arousal reduction reframes helping as escaping from one's own discomfort, not benefiting the other. It is self-interested (helping to relieve your own distress), not other-focused.

questions.q: What is social esteem / self-rewards attraction as a pro-egoistic explanation?
options: The view that society should reward egoistic behavior
The claim that people help to gain social approval or internal self-reward
The theory that egoism is socially acceptable
The idea that external rewards determine moral rightness
The view that self-reward contradicts altruism
questions.explain: This pro-egoistic explanation recasts helping as motivated by gaining social status, approval, or internal satisfaction — all self-interested motives. The act may look altruistic but is driven by the agent's desire for esteem.

questions.q: What is self-punishment avoidance as a pro-egoistic explanation for helping?
options: The idea that egoists are punished by society
The claim that people help to avoid guilt or self-blame — a self-interested motive to escape internal punishment
A form of altruism where one helps to prevent others' suffering
The view that punishment is not justified in an egoistic system
A theory that all behavior is motivated by fear
questions.explain: Self-punishment avoidance reinterprets helping as motivated by the agent's desire to escape guilt or self-blame. Even though it looks other-focused, the real motive is self-interested (avoiding internal punishment).

questions.q: How does Ethical Egoism respond to the objection that it is not a genuine moral theory?
options: By showing that all moral theories are equally valid
By distinguishing Ethical Egoism from Rational Egoism and emphasizing that EE competes with other moral theories in the same normative domain
By proving that Psychological Egoism is true
By arguing that morality does not exist
By rejecting the concept of obligation
questions.explain: The lecture notes that EE and RE are cousins but apply to different domains. EE addresses morality (what is right/wrong), while RE addresses rationality. This distinction helps EE claim legitimacy as a moral theory competing with other positions.

lectures.title: Lecture 6: Kant on the Idea of Duty

questions.q: According to Kant, on what grounds is the moral law based?
options: On human nature and natural desires
On pure practical reason common to all rational agents
On the empirical facts of human happiness
On cultural traditions and social customs
On religious revelation
questions.explain: Kant explicitly grounds morality in pure practical reason, not human nature. The correct answer reflects his key insight that moral law holds for all rational agents, not just humans. Confusing Kant's view with happiness-based theories is a common exam trap.

questions.q: What is a Hypothetical Imperative, and how does it differ from the Categorical Imperative?
options: A Hypothetical Imperative is unconditional and applies to all rational agents, while a Categorical Imperative depends on contingent desires
A Hypothetical Imperative depends on contingent desires and chosen ends, while a Categorical Imperative is unconditional and binds regardless of ends
A Hypothetical Imperative prohibits certain actions, while a Categorical Imperative requires them
A Hypothetical Imperative concerns morality, while a Categorical Imperative concerns prudence
Both are equally binding moral commands
questions.explain: The defining feature of a Hypothetical Imperative is its dependence on contingent desires (if you want E, and A is necessary for E, then do A). The Categorical Imperative binds unconditionally. Many students reverse these definitions.

questions.q: What does Kant mean by 'ends in themselves' in the context of rational nature?
options: Ends that are chosen for the sake of achieving other ends
Ends that have unconditional value independent of any choice or desire
Ends that are merely instrumental to happiness
Ends that conflict with the Categorical Imperative
Ends that require empirical verification
questions.explain: Ends in themselves possess intrinsic, unconditional value by virtue of being rational. This is foundational to Kant's ethics. Ends adopted by desire, by contrast, have only conditional worth as objects of choice.

questions.q: The Formula of Humanity prohibits treating persons merely as means. Which scenario violates this prohibition?
options: A friend willingly agrees to drive you to the airport knowing this is a means to your end
A customer buys coffee from a barista who willingly provides the service
A mugger forces a victim at gunpoint to hand over their wallet
A doctor prescribes medication that causes temporary discomfort in order to cure illness
A parent asks a child to do chores as a means to teach responsibility
questions.explain: The mugger scenario treats the victim as a mere means without respect for their autonomy or consent. The key distinction is that the friend, barista, and child in other options give consent or participate willingly. The exam trap is confusing 'means' with 'mere means' — using someone as a means is permissible if they are also treated as an end.

questions.q: What are the two main parts of the Formula of Humanity?
options: The negative part (never treat as mere means) and the positive part (promote self-perfection and others' happiness)
Autonomy and heteronomy
The theoretical part and the practical part
The universal part and the particular part
The rational part and the empirical part
questions.explain: The Formula of Humanity has a negative arm (prohibiting treatment as mere means) and a positive arm (requiring promotion of certain ends). This structure is explicit in Kant's text and the lecture notes.

questions.q: Kant identifies a hierarchy of duties in his moral system. Which of the following correctly describes this hierarchy?
options: Duties move from abstract general principles to context-specific applications through casuistry
All duties are equally binding with no distinction
General principles apply directly to cases without need for further specification
Imperfect duties always rank above perfect duties
Duties are determined solely by consequences in each situation
questions.explain: Kant uses casuistry to move from universal moral principles to particular situations, recognizing that application requires judgment. When duties conflict, 'the stronger ground of obligation prevails.'

questions.q: What distinguishes a perfect duty from an imperfect duty?
options: Perfect duties are theoretical while imperfect duties are practical
Perfect duties must never (or always) be performed fully with no discretion, while imperfect duties allow latitude in how and when performed
Perfect duties apply only to oneself while imperfect duties apply to others
Perfect duties are always easy to fulfill while imperfect duties are difficult
Both are identical in their binding force
questions.explain: The core distinction concerns discretion: perfect duties (like 'do not lie') allow no exceptions, while imperfect duties (like 'develop your talents') allow latitude. A common exam trap is treating 'imperfect' as 'optional' — imperfect duties still bind, just with flexibility in execution.

questions.q: According to Kant's system, what is the foundation of the duty of self-perfection?
options: The capacity to set oneself any end whatsoever — this capacity is what characterizes humanity
The desire for personal happiness
The requirement to treat others as ends
The laws of nature that govern human development
The social contract established among rational beings
questions.explain: Kant grounds the duty of self-perfection in the distinctively human capacity to set ends — by protecting and promoting humanity in oneself, we must develop this capacity. The desire for happiness is mentioned separately as a natural wish, not the foundation of the duty.

questions.q: The Formula of Universal Law requires that we act only on maxims we can will as universal laws of nature. What is a maxim in this context?
options: A rule set by the government
An objective moral law that applies to all persons
A subjective principle of volition on which an agent acts intentionally, having the form 'I will ________, if/when ________ in order to ________'
A consequence-based rule that maximizes utility
A religious or cultural commandment
questions.explain: Kant's maxim has a specific semantic structure — it includes the agent's intended action, the condition, and the purpose. Understanding this structure is essential to applying the universalizability test correctly.

questions.q: In the false-promising example, why is making a false promise wrong according to the Formula of Universal Law?
options: Because it violates religious law
Because it causes unhappiness to the victim
Because the maxim, if universalized, would collapse the very institution of promising — creating a self-contradiction
Because Kant personally disapproved of dishonesty
Because it violates a perfect duty to maximize others' welfare
questions.explain: The false-promising case illustrates the logical contradiction that arises when universalizing: if everyone made false promises, no one would believe promises anymore, so the practice would cease — the agent cannot rationally will this outcome. This is not mere empirical consequence but logical self-defeat.

questions.q: How does the selfishness example differ from the false-promising example in terms of the type of contradiction involved?
options: The selfishness example involves a logical contradiction, the false-promising example involves an empirical contradiction
Both involve the same type of contradiction and are indistinguishable
The selfishness example fails due to conflicting rationality maxims rather than logical contradiction; the agent cannot will both to be selfish and simultaneously to be helped by others when in need
The selfishness example is actually not a real contradiction at all
The false-promising example is weaker because it relies on consequences rather than reason
questions.explain: The selfishness maxim does not create a logical contradiction in the institution itself (unlike promising). Rather, one cannot rationally will both the maxim of selfishness and the simultaneous maxim 'I will be helped when I need it.' This shows Kant's test goes deeper than institutional collapse.

questions.q: According to Kant's theory of right conduct based on the Formula of Humanity, when is an action obligatory?
options: When it produces the greatest happiness
When failing to perform it would treat oneself or others merely as means to a non-moral end
When the law commands it
When it follows the maxim of commission
When it is universalizable
questions.explain: The Humanity formulation defines obligatory actions as those whose omission would fail to respect humanity. This is distinct from the FUL criterion. The two formulations are not obviously equivalent, a key exam point.

questions.q: According to Kant's theory of right conduct based on the Formula of Universal Law, an action is wrong if:
options: One cannot universalize the maxim of omission
It causes unhappiness
One cannot universalize the maxim of commission associated with that action
It violates imperfect duties
It is not commanded by reason
questions.explain: Under FUL, wrongness is determined by the inability to universalize the maxim of commission (doing the action), while obligatoriness is determined by the inability to universalize the maxim of omission. This commission/omission distinction is crucial and often confused.

questions.q: What is the exam trap regarding the relationship between the universalizability test and rule consequentialism?
options: They are exactly the same theory
The universalizability test is NOT rule consequentialism — it is not about whether an action produces the best outcomes when universalized
The universalizability test evaluates actions by aggregate outcomes, just as rule consequentialism does
Rule consequentialism is more strict than Kant's theory
Kant explicitly endorsed rule consequentialism
questions.explain: A critical exam point: Kant's universalizability test is not about consequences or outcomes. It concerns whether a maxim can be rationally willed as a universal law. Conflating these theories misses the logical structure of Kant's argument.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a false negative objection to the Formula of Universal Law?
options: 'Whenever the stock market climbs another 200 points, I will withdraw all my savings' — deemed impermissible by FUL but intuitively not morally wrong
'I will make false promises whenever I need money' — wrong under FUL but intuitively wrong
'I will help others in need' — clearly permissible
'I will always tell the truth' — clearly obligatory
'I will develop my talents' — clearly a duty
questions.explain: A false negative occurs when FUL condemns an action that is not intuitively wrong. The stock market maxim seems universalizable (too specific to create contradiction) but is deemed impermissible, which seems too strict.

questions.q: Kant holds that all persons have dignity and deserve respect. Which statement best captures his view on this?
options: Only virtuous persons deserve respect
Only persons with pure practical reason deserve dignity
One cannot deny respect to even a vicious person as a human being, even if he makes himself unworthy by his deeds
Respect is earned through good behavior and happiness
Respect is based on social status or achievement
questions.explain: Kant's view is radical: autonomy itself is what confers dignity, and all rational beings possess it. Vicious deeds may make one unworthy of respect in a derivative sense, but the person retains fundamental dignity as a rational agent.

questions.q: What role does the 'good will' play in Kant's conception of moral worth?
options: It is the only unconditionally good thing and is marked by disposition to act from duty alone
It is optional for moral agents
It must be accompanied by good consequences
It is secondary to actual happiness
It depends on natural inclinations
questions.explain: The famous opening of the Groundwork: 'It is impossible to think of anything at all in the world, or indeed even beyond it, that could be considered good without limitation except a good will.' Moral worth flows from disposition to act from duty, not from results.

questions.q: According to Kant's doctrine of the highest good, what two components must it contain?
options: Virtue and pleasure alone
Possession of virtuous character and happiness befitting one's virtue
Happiness and power
Knowledge and happiness
Freedom and equality
questions.explain: Kant insists the highest good is NOT virtue alone (that would be grim) nor mere happiness alone (that would be amoral). The two must be conjoined: virtue with proportionate happiness.

questions.q: Why does Kant believe immortality is a necessary postulate for achieving the highest good?
options: Because God guarantees it in religious texts
Because achieving the highest good requires endless moral progress, which requires continuous existence of the same rational being
Because empirical experience proves the soul is immortal
Because finite beings cannot be rational
Because happiness requires infinite time
questions.explain: Immortality is postulated as a practical, not theoretical, necessity. Endless progress toward perfection requires an endless existence. This is a presupposition of moral practice, not a cognizable truth.

questions.q: What is Kant's position on whether we can have knowledge of God's existence?
options: We can prove God exists through pure reason
We cannot cognize God — God is not an object of sense experience; the postulate is practical, not theoretical
We can know God through sense experience
God's existence is a matter of pure speculation
Kant rejects all reference to God
questions.explain: A critical exam point: Kant denies that we can have theoretical knowledge of God. The postulate of God is practical — required for moral coherence — not a knowledge claim. This distinguishes his position from metaphysical theism.

questions.q: Which distinction is essential to understanding whether an action violates the Formula of Humanity?
options: The distinction between perfect and imperfect duties
The distinction between regarding someone as a mere means and actually treating them as a mere means in one's action
The distinction between maxims of commission and omission
The distinction between autonomy and heteronomy
The distinction between empirical and a priori knowledge
questions.explain: The gangster buying coffee regards the seller as a mere means but does not treat him as such in the transaction. Many students miss this subtle distinction. One's attitude and one's conduct can diverge morally.

questions.q: Kant argues that moral law applies to all rational agents, not just humans. What implication does this have?
options: Non-human rational beings, if they exist, are equally bound by the moral law
Moral law is grounded in facts about human biology
Only humans are capable of rationality
Moral law has no universal application
Non-rational creatures also have moral status
questions.explain: Kant's universalism extends the scope of morality beyond human nature. The moral law holds for any rational agent. This follows from grounding ethics in pure practical reason rather than human nature.

questions.q: How do vices and virtues relate to Kant's system of duties?
options: Virtues are attitudes that facilitate fulfilling our duties; vices are attitudes that hinder fulfilling our duties
Vices and virtues are external regulations imposed by society
Vices and virtues are optional refinements beyond duty
They play no role in Kant's ethics
Only virtues correspond to duties
questions.explain: Vices and virtues are dispositions — inner attitudes — that either enable or obstruct our ability to fulfill moral duties. Virtue (e.g., courage) is the inner strength to resist temptation and act from duty.

questions.q: In the Lizbeth and Tom case, Lizbeth hides Tom from murderers but must lie to protect him. How does Kant resolve this conflict of duties?
options: Lying is always absolutely wrong, so Lizbeth should not lie
The stronger ground of obligation prevails — protecting an innocent person's life outweighs the duty not to lie
There is no conflict because protecting life is obviously wrong
Consequentialist reasoning determines which duty wins
All duties are equally binding and cannot be weighed against each other
questions.explain: Kant explicitly says 'The stronger ground of obligation prevails.' This case illustrates that perfect duties are not truly absolute when they conflict — the higher-order obligation to respect humanity can override a particular perfect duty.

questions.q: What is the key difference between how the universalizability test applies to the false-promising and selfishness cases?
options: Both create the same type of contradiction
Selfishness is not subject to the universalizability test
False promising is not actually wrong while selfishness is
False promising creates an institutional contradiction; selfishness creates a rational contradiction with a simultaneous maxim
False promising involves imperfect duties while selfishness involves perfect duties
questions.explain: The false-promising case shows that universalizing the maxim destroys the practice it presupposes (institutional collapse). The selfishness case shows that the agent cannot rationally will both the selfish maxim and its inverse (rational contradiction). These are distinct types of failure.

questions.q: According to Kant, what must accompany the possession of virtuous character to constitute the highest good?
options: The approval of society
Happiness proportionate to one's virtue
Complete absence of desire
Knowledge of metaphysical truths
Political power and influence
questions.explain: Kant explicitly rejects the idea that an impartial observer could take delight in seeing uninterrupted prosperity in a person graced with no good will. Virtue requires accompaniment by fitting happiness.

questions.q: Which of the following best explains why Kant rejects grounding morality in human nature?
options: Human nature is too variable and different across cultures
Moral law must hold for all rational agents, not just humans; thus it must be grounded in pure practical reason, not empirical facts about humans
Human nature is too selfish and base to be a moral foundation
Kant personally disliked human nature
Nature is inherently immoral
questions.explain: The logical structure of Kant's argument: if moral law applies universally to any rational agent, it cannot be grounded in facts specific to human nature. Pure practical reason is the only universally applicable foundation.

questions.q: What do the Categorical Imperative's two main formulas — Formula of Humanity and Formula of Universal Law — have in common?
options: They are identical and always yield the same verdicts
They apply only to perfect duties
They are both attempts to articulate the structure of unconditional moral requirements, though they provide different criteria for right action
Only one of them is genuinely binding
They are based on consequentialist reasoning
questions.explain: A subtle but important exam point: FH and FUL are presented as two formulations of one categorical imperative, yet they are not obviously equivalent. The lecture notes flag that distinguishing these formulations is important.

questions.q: According to Kant's system, which of the following is NOT a reason for postulating God?
options: To explain how happiness can be proportionate to virtue
To ensure the universe obeys mathematical laws
To provide a cause adequate to produce the effect of virtue accompanied by happiness
To ground the coherence of moral practice
Because the highest good requires more than human powers to achieve
questions.explain: Kant explicitly postulates God to explain how moral effort can result in proportionate happiness — it requires a supernatural cause. Mathematical order in the universe is not his reasoning here.

questions.q: In Kant's view, why is the distinction between regarding someone as a mere means versus treating them as a mere means morally significant?
options: Because what matters in morality is external action, not internal attitude
Because regarding someone wrongly is worse than treating them wrongly
Because moral wrongness concerns how one treats others in action, not merely one's internal attitudes toward them
Because all internal attitudes are equally wrong
Because Kant believed attitudes are irrelevant to morality
questions.explain: Kant's position is subtle: a vicious gangster may regard people as mere instruments internally, yet in a fair transaction, he does not treat the person wrongly. The action is permissible even though the attitude is corrupt. This shows that respect for autonomy in action is independent of motives.

questions.q: According to the lecture, which of the following best describes a virtue?
options: A relatively fixed trait of character acquired through practice and exercise
A momentary impulse or emotional reaction
An innate natural ability that humans are born with
A set of explicit rules that govern moral behavior
A subjective preference determined entirely by individual choice
questions.explain: Virtues are described as relatively fixed traits of character, not momentary impulses, and crucially, they are acquired through practice and exercise, not innate. This contrasts directly with the exam trap that virtues are 'naturally endowed excellences.'

questions.q: The intellectual component of a virtue involves which of the following?
options: The emotional intensity with which one feels the virtue
Correct beliefs about when the virtue is appropriately expressed
The physical ability to perform the virtue in public settings
The social status gained from displaying the virtue
The unconscious habits developed through repetition alone
questions.explain: The intellectual component concerns correct beliefs — for honesty, it means understanding when telling the truth is appropriate. The affective component handles feeling/emotion, and the motivational-behavioral component covers action.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed as a cardinal virtue in the Greek tradition?
options: Wisdom
Courage
Generosity
Temperance
Justice
questions.explain: The four cardinal virtues in the Greek tradition are wisdom, courage, temperance, and justice. Generosity is not among them. The Christian tradition adds faith, hope, and love, but generosity still does not appear as a cardinal virtue in either list.

questions.q: Aristotle's claim that all human activities aim at some end or good is called which of the following?
options: Deontological reasoning
The teleological premise
The function argument
The doctrine of the mean
The principle of subsidiarity
questions.explain: The teleological (goal-directed) premise underpins Aristotle's ethics: all activities aim at some end or good. This is foundational to his argument about the highest good, eudaimonia.

questions.q: In Aristotle's Function Argument, the function of humans is grounded in which distinctive characteristic?
options: Physical strength and endurance
Emotional sensitivity and vulnerability
Rationality and the exercise of reason
Social status and hierarchical rank
The capacity to accumulate material possessions
questions.explain: The Function Argument identifies rationality as the distinctive feature of humans. The highest good for humans is therefore the activity of the soul in accordance with rationality, guided by virtue.

questions.q: Which statement most accurately reflects Aristotle's position on virtue and eudaimonia (flourishing)?
options: Virtue is both necessary and sufficient for eudaimonia
Virtue is necessary but not sufficient; external goods also matter
Virtue is sufficient but not necessary for eudaimonia
Virtue has no direct connection to eudaimonia
Eudaimonia can be achieved without any virtue at all
questions.explain: Aristotle holds that virtue is necessary but not sufficient for eudaimonia — you need external goods (health, wealth, good fortune) as well. The Stoics, by contrast, claim virtue is both necessary and sufficient, which is a classic exam confusion point.

questions.q: According to Aristotle's Doctrine of the Mean, the intermediate condition between excess and deficiency is determined by which of the following?
options: A fixed numerical average applicable to all persons
The personal preferences of the individual agent
Practical intelligence (phronesis) relative to persons and contexts
The majority opinion of the community
The written rules of a particular society
questions.explain: The doctrine of the mean is not arithmetically fixed — the intermediate condition is relative to persons and contexts, determined by phronesis (practical wisdom). What is moderate courage for a soldier differs from what is moderate courage for a scholar.

questions.q: Phronesis (practical intelligence) is best described as which of the following?
options: A higher-order virtue that governs the exercise of all other virtues
The capacity to calculate mathematical problems accurately
The ability to understand complex written texts and theories
An innate talent that requires no development
The skill to persuade others through eloquent speech
questions.explain: Phronesis is described as a higher-order virtue — the capacity to determine the right manner of feeling and action in contexts requiring a virtuous response. It comes only with life experience and distinguishes the morally mature adult.

questions.q: The Unity of Virtues doctrine claims that virtues are interdependent. This means which of the following?
options: All virtues are identical to one another
Truly possessing one virtue requires possessing all others
Virtues can be ranked in complete isolation from each other
Having one virtue makes having others impossible
Virtues have no meaningful relationship to each other
questions.explain: Unity of virtues does NOT mean virtues are identical. Rather, it means they are interdependent — truly having one virtue entails having the others. The exam trap is confusing interdependence with identity.

questions.q: In Virtue Ethics, what is the primary foundational claim about the relationship between character and right conduct?
options: Right conduct determines character
Character and conduct are unrelated
Facts about virtuous agents and their character are more basic than facts about right conduct
Right conduct can be determined without reference to character
Character is only relevant after actions have been evaluated
questions.explain: VE's core claim is that facts about virtuous agents — their character traits and how they influence reactions — are more basic than facts about right conduct. Character is foundational, not derivative.

questions.q: According to the qualified agent-based version of Virtue Ethics, an action is obligatory if and only if which of the following is true?
options: Most people would perform the action in that circumstance
Any ideally virtuous agent would not fail to perform it in that circumstance
The agent performing it stands to benefit personally
The action conforms to written laws or regulations
The action receives approval from religious authorities
questions.explain: The qualified agent-based criterion defines obligatory actions as those an ideally virtuous agent would not fail to do. This differs from the definition of 'wrong' (no ideal agent would do) and 'optional' (ideal agent might or might not do).

questions.q: Why does Virtue Ethics' plurality of cardinal virtues create moral conflicts?
options: Because cardinal virtues contradict the doctrine of the mean
Because some virtues are more important than others
Because each virtue yields a virtue rule, and multiple relevant virtues may indicate incompatible courses of action
Because people are naturally unable to practice multiple virtues
Because the community cannot agree on virtue definitions
questions.explain: VE does not eliminate moral conflict by having no fundamental rules — rather, its plurality of cardinal virtues (each with its own virtue rule) creates its own conflicts when virtues point toward incompatible actions.

questions.q: The reforming liar counterexample to Virtue Ethics shows which of the following?
options: That virtue is worthless as a moral concept
That the ideal agent criterion fails to capture self-improvement strategies as morally correct
That liars can never become virtuous people
That virtue ethics is superior to all other moral theories
That self-improvement is impossible under virtue ethics
questions.explain: A mendacious person's regimen of writing down lies and reflecting on them is clearly right and necessary, yet it is not what an ideally virtuous agent would do. This shows the original VE criterion's failure — the counterexample targets the action criterion, not virtue generally.

questions.q: The obstinate-person counterexample reveals a flaw in which revised VE criterion?
options: The criterion that an action is obligatory iff an ideal agent would advise one not to fail to do it
The claim that virtue requires external goods
The definition of eudaimonia as happiness
The doctrine of the mean
The principle of subsidiarity
questions.explain: In this counterexample, an obstinate person does the opposite of whatever is advised. An ideal agent, knowing this, might strategically advise false advice to get the desired result — so what an ideal agent would advise is not what the person ought to do.

questions.q: Care Ethics was inspired by which psychologist's 1982 work, In a Different Voice?
options: Carol Gilligan
Lawrence Kohlberg
Jean Piaget
Nel Noddings
Helene Deutsch
questions.explain: Carol Gilligan's 1982 book In a Different Voice inspired Care Ethics. She argued that personal relationships — between parents and children, siblings, friends, and spouses — are paradigmatic for all morality.

questions.q: According to Care Ethics, which of the following is the defining moral feature of personal relationships?
options: Care as the central moral feature
Contractual obligation
Rational impartiality
Legal compliance
Economic exchange
questions.explain: Care Ethics identifies care as the defining moral feature of personal relationships (between parents and children, siblings, friends, spouses). These relationships are paradigmatic for understanding all morality.

questions.q: In the comparison between Justice and Care perspectives, inequality is to the Justice perspective as which of the following is to the Care perspective?
options: Impartiality
Disconnection and abandonment
Individual rights
Legal fairness
Rational consistency
questions.explain: The Justice perspective treats inequality as the central issue, while the Care perspective identifies disconnection and abandonment as central moral problems. This reflects their different conceptions of moral priority.

questions.q: Which pair of terms correctly captures the distinction between the two senses of care in Care Ethics?
options: Legal and moral
Theoretical and practical
Caring about (attitudinal) and caring for (practical engagement)
Individual and collective
Personal and impersonal
questions.explain: Care Ethics distinguishes caring about (being invested in a thing or person — an attitudinal state) from caring for (practical actions in the context of care). Both senses are essential to a full account of care.

questions.q: Care Ethics does NOT restrict moral care responsibilities to existing personal relationships because which of the following is true?
options: Personal relationships are morally unimportant
All relationships have equal moral weight
Advocates argue that responsibilities of care are global and should extend beyond one's immediate circle
Care cannot be extended to strangers at all
Distant relationships are more important than close ones
questions.explain: While personal relationships are paradigmatic for Care Ethics, advocates argue that responsibilities of care are global — one ought to extend care to others beyond one's immediate circle. This addresses the potential narrowness of the theory.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of Joan Tronto's five care stages?
options: Attentiveness
Responsibility
Reciprocity
Competence
Solidarity
questions.explain: Tronto's five stages are: Attentiveness (Caring About), Responsibility (Taking Care Of), Competence (Care-Giving), Responsiveness (Care-Receiving), and Solidarity (Caring With). Reciprocity is not among the five stages.

questions.q: The stage of Attentiveness in Tronto's framework is also called which of the following?
options: Caring About
Taking Care Of
Care-Giving
Care-Receiving
Caring With
questions.explain: Attentiveness is paired with 'Caring About' — it involves recognizing that a need exists and overcoming moral blindness. Each of Tronto's five stages has a specific paired activity form that students often confuse.

questions.q: In Tronto's framework, the Responsiveness stage involves which of the following?
options: Recognizing that a need exists
Ensuring the care provided meets the need
Considering the receiver's perspective and being alert to power abuse
Recognizing care as a collective responsibility
Shifting from individual to group action
questions.explain: Responsiveness (Care-Receiving) means considering the receiver's perspective and being alert to potential abuses of power. This stage emphasizes the dignity and agency of the care recipient.

questions.q: According to Stephanie Collins (2020), which of the following is NOT covered by Care Ethics as a complete moral theory?
options: Duties arising from making promises or contracts
Duties arising from personal relationships
Duties of attentiveness and care
Duties to recognize others' needs
Duties of emotional responsiveness
questions.explain: Collins argues that Care Ethics does not cover duties arising from harming others, receiving benefits, making promises and contracts, or non-interference duties. These remain outside the scope of CE, which is why it is not a complete moral theory.

questions.q: What is the core requirement of the Dependency Principle in Care Ethics?
options: When an important interest is unfulfilled, you are capable, and doing so is not too costly — you have a responsibility to fulfill it
Help anyone who asks, regardless of cost to yourself
Always prioritize the needs of strangers over your own family
Provide unlimited care to all persons in need
Never refuse a request for help
questions.explain: The Dependency Principle (Collins) requires three conditions: the interest must be important, you must be capable of fulfilling it, AND doing so must not be too costly. This is not an unlimited duty to help — it respects both the sufferer's need and the caregiver's limits.

questions.q: The Principle of Subsidiarity in Care Ethics emphasizes which of the following?
options: Reducing the overall amount of care provided in society
Centralizing care delivery to professional institutions
Shifting actual delivery of care to the most local and personal levels possible
Creating new bureaucratic organizations for care
Eliminating personal relationships from moral consideration
questions.explain: Subsidiarity (Engster) means shifting care delivery to the most local and personal levels whenever possible — care for others by enabling them to care for themselves. It is not about reducing care, but about respecting agency and autonomy.

questions.q: Both the Dependency Principle and Principle of Subsidiarity in Care Ethics must be guided by which of the following?
options: Emotional attunement (共鳴/調諧)
Written laws and regulations
Rational impartial reasoning
Economic efficiency calculations
Majority community consensus
questions.explain: Application of both care ethics principles must be guided by emotional attunement — sensitivity to the particular needs, perspectives, and contexts of those involved. This distinguishes CE's character from impartial rule-based approaches.

questions.q: Which of the following best explains why the three components of virtue (intellectual, affective, motivational-behavioral) are all necessary?
options: A virtue requires correct beliefs, emotional disposition, and behavioral tendency to function fully
They are three different names for the same single capability
Only one component is truly necessary; the others are optional
The affective component makes the other two unnecessary
The intellectual component alone is sufficient for any virtue
questions.explain: Using honesty as an example: the intellectual component is understanding when truth-telling is appropriate; the affective component is approval of honesty; the motivational-behavioral component is the tendency to tell the truth. All three work together to constitute the virtue.

questions.q: In the military rationing example used to illustrate the Unity of Virtues, why does lacking temperance undermine justice?
options: Because a truly just person must also be temperate; without temperance she would be disposed to take more than her fair share, undermining justice
Because temperance is more important than justice
Because justice and temperance are the same virtue
Because military contexts never require justice
Because rationing has nothing to do with virtue
questions.explain: This example demonstrates that virtues are interdependent: a person cannot be truly just while lacking temperance, since without temperance she would take more than her fair share, violating justice in the rationing scenario.

questions.q: Care Ethics is explicitly described as which of the following type of theory?
options: Not a complete moral theory — it does not cover non-interference duties, promise-based duties, or duties from harm
A comprehensive theory covering all moral duties
The only correct theory of morality
A theory that replaces all justice-based duties
A theory that proves virtue ethics is wrong
questions.explain: Collins (2020, 98) makes clear that Care Ethics is not a complete moral theory. It focuses on care relationships but leaves gaps regarding duties from harming, receiving benefits, promises, contracts, and non-interference.

questions.q: What distinguished Aristotle's position on virtue from that of the Stoics?
options: Aristotle believed virtue alone cannot guarantee eudaimonia; Stoics believed virtue alone is both necessary and sufficient
Aristotle believed virtue is both necessary and sufficient for eudaimonia; Stoics believed virtue is only necessary
Aristotle rejected virtue entirely; Stoics embraced it fully
Stoics focused on external goods; Aristotle ignored them
There was no meaningful difference between their views
questions.explain: This is a critical distinction and a frequent exam trap: Aristotle says virtue is necessary but not sufficient (external goods matter); the Stoics say virtue is both necessary and sufficient (virtue alone guarantees eudaimonia). This difference captures fundamentally different views on human flourishing.

lectures.title: Lecture 8: Questioning the Need for Principles

questions.q: Which of the following best defines the core contrast between Generalism and Particularism in moral philosophy?
options: Generalism depends on general principles; Particularism depends on context-sensitive features of particular cases
Generalism is more objective; Particularism is purely subjective opinion
Generalism applies only to professional ethics; Particularism applies to personal morality
Generalism rejects all moral generalizations; Particularism accepts them
Generalism is utilitarian; Particularism is deontological
questions.explain: The lecture defines Generalism as depending on general principles and Particularism as depending on context-sensitive features of particular cases. Particularism does not mean moral relativism or pure subjectivism.

questions.q: Principle Eliminativism (PE) and Principle Abstinence (PA) are logically independent. Which statement correctly describes this relationship?
options: PE entails PA in all cases
One can hold PE without PA, or PA without PE — they do not entail each other
PA entails PE, but not vice versa
They are the same position with different names
Neither can be true if the other is false
questions.explain: PE and PA are logically independent. PE says no correct moral principles exist; PA says agents should not rely solely on principles for guidance. A student might reject PE but still accept PA.

questions.q: What is the fundamental difference between an Absolute Principle (AP) and a Contributory Principle (CP)?
options: AP applies to all people; CP applies only to professionals
AP uses deductive logic; CP uses inductive reasoning
AP states a certain action is always right or wrong; CP states only that a feature counts for or against but can be outweighed
AP is relative to culture; CP is universal
AP is about consequences; CP is about duties
questions.explain: AP is decisive — once a feature is present, the verdict is fixed. CP is defeasible — it states a feature counts for or against but can be outweighed by other considerations.

questions.q: Why do Generalists believe that principles serve a crucial role in moral theory?
options: Principles eliminate the need for moral reasoning
Principles guarantee that all moral judgments are correct
Principles provide both explanatory and practical guidance for moral agents
Principles make morality subjective rather than objective
Principles replace the need for moral intuition
questions.explain: Generalists identify two roles: the explanatory role (knowing why an action is wrong) and the practical role (principles provide authority of guidance). These roles are essential to coherent moral theory.

questions.q: The Universal Relevance Thesis states that morally relevant features maintain their relevance across all cases. How does this thesis relate to Reasons Atomism?
options: Universal Relevance is incompatible with Atomism
Atomism is only applicable when Universal Relevance fails
Both assume that moral features do not become irrelevant by context — atomism extends this to claim polarity remains fixed
Universal Relevance makes Atomism impossible
They are unrelated positions
questions.explain: Reasons Atomism holds that the moral contribution of a feature is fixed independently of context. Universal Relevance is a prerequisite for Atomism; together they form the generalist view that moral facts are context-independent.

questions.q: According to Reasons Holism, what is the central variability claim about moral features?
options: All features are morally irrelevant in some contexts
Moral features become stronger as they are applied repeatedly
A feature that counts in favour in one case may count against in another; the moral contribution depends on context
The moral weight of a feature is determined only by the agent's intentions
Moral context never influences the status of a feature
questions.explain: Reasons Holism claims the moral contribution of a feature may depend on context. A feature might be a reason in one case and no reason in another. This variability puts pressure on fixed, principle-like systems.

questions.q: In McNaughton's public hanging example, what does the sadistic pleasure illustrate?
options: Pleasure is never a morally relevant feature
The same feature (pleasure) can function as a reason against an action when its context is sadistic, illustrating reversal
Outweighing occurs when pleasure is insufficient to justify execution
The principle that all pleasure is morally wrong
Context is irrelevant to determining moral status
questions.explain: The pleasure spectators would enjoy is normally a reason in favour. But in the context of sadistic pleasure, the same feature reverses — it becomes a reason against. This shows polarity can flip depending on context.

questions.q: How does the particularist view of reversal differ from the Rossian (generalist) view in the public hanging example?
options: Particularists say the pleasure's polarity flips; Rossians say it remains positive but is outweighed by cruelty
Particularists reject pleasure as a moral feature entirely
Rossians say the pleasure is silenced; Particularists say it is outweighed
Both views agree that pleasure always counts in favour
There is no difference between the two positions
questions.explain: The Rossian grants that pleasure still counts positively but is outweighed by cruelty. The particularist argues the pleasure does not count positively at all — the moral contribution itself changes. This is a common exam error.

questions.q: What does it mean for a feature to be 'silenced' in the context of moral reasoning?
options: A feature is outweighed by stronger reasons
A feature that usually matters becomes morally irrelevant in a particular context
A feature is explicitly prohibited by a moral rule
A feature is understood by the agent but ignored anyway
A feature loses its definition in context
questions.explain: Silencing occurs when a feature that normally serves as a reason becomes irrelevant. The promise to help someone cheat is silenced — the promise does not give a reason to cheat in this case. Silencing differs from outweighing fundamentally.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly identifies the four possible statuses of a moral feature?
options: Always relevant, sometimes relevant, never relevant, or contextually irrelevant
Relevant in favour, relevant against, morally irrelevant in context, or relevant in a way that depends on other features
Positive, negative, neutral, or ambiguous
Decisive, defeasible, outweighed, or silenced
Principle-based, intuition-based, consequentialist, or deontological
questions.explain: The notes illustrate this with lying: it can be relevant in favour, relevant against, morally irrelevant, or relevant in a way dependent on other features. These four statuses capture the particularist view of feature variability.

questions.q: What are the two main strategies that Generalists use to respond to the challenge of Reasons Holism?
options: Principle Eliminativism and Principle Abstinence
Atomistic Specification and Holistic Accommodation
Reversal and Silencing
Universal Relevance and Polarity
Deontological and Consequentialist approaches
questions.explain: Atomistic Specification involves adding conditions to block counterexamples. Holistic Accommodation accepts reasons holism but insists principles are still possible. These are two different generalist responses to the particularist challenge.

questions.q: In the Atomistic Specification strategy, how does the generalist attempt to handle the promise example?
options: By eliminating promises as a morally relevant feature
By adding conditions like 'the promise was not coerced' and 'the promised act is not immoral' to make the principle more precise
By accepting that promises always create moral obligations
By agreeing that promises should never create reasons to act
By rejecting the principle-based approach entirely
questions.explain: The simple principle becomes specified with additional conditions. The particularist objection is that these extra conditions are enablers and disablers, not additional reasons, so the strategy does not save genuinely atomistic generalism.

questions.q: How do particularists distinguish between 'reasons,' 'enablers,' and 'disablers'?
options: All three are synonymous with 'moral principle'
Reasons override enablers and disablers
Reasons are the actual moral considerations; enablers allow a reason to function; disablers prevent it from functioning
Disablers are the same as reasons with reversed polarity
Enablers and disablers do not exist in particularist theory
questions.explain: When a generalist adds conditions like 'the promise was not coerced,' they are adding enablers (conditions that allow a consideration to function as a reason), not additional reasons. This hidden holism undermines the claim to save atomism.

questions.q: What is Holistic Generalism (HG), and how does it respond to Reasons Holism?
options: HG rejects reasons holism entirely
HG accepts reasons holism while insisting that principles are still possible by building context-sensitivity into principle structure
HG eliminates all moral principles
HG argues that context never affects moral features
HG claims that all moral judgments are subjective
questions.explain: HG concedes that a feature's moral contribution depends on context but maintains that principles can accommodate this through holistic formulation. This shows that accepting Reasons Holism does not entail Principle Eliminativism.

questions.q: What does 'Double Defeasibility' in Holistic Generalism consist of?
options: Two mutually exclusive moral principles
A morally significant feature, a holism clause addressing context-sensitivity, and an overriding clause for moral conflict
The ability to be wrong in two different ways
A feature that reverses and is silenced simultaneously
Reasons and disablers combined into one concept
questions.explain: HG principles have three components: the morally significant feature, the holism clause (considering potential silencing or reversal), and the overriding clause (allowing other reasons to collectively outweigh). These make the principle defeasible in two ways.

questions.q: How does the particularist method of moral explanation differ from the Holistic Generalist method?
options: Both methods are identical
Particularists use narration showing how concrete features add up; HG uses subsumption under general principles
Particularists use principles; HG uses case-by-case analysis
HG rejects all explanation; Particularists provide systematic theories
There is no meaningful difference between the approaches
questions.explain: HG explains by subsuming particular cases under a general principle; particularism explains by narration, showing how the morally relevant features of this concrete situation add up. This distinction reveals that even holistic principles may not be necessary for moral explanation.

questions.q: What does Principle Abstinence (PA) claim about the role of principles in moral deliberation?
options: All moral principles should be eliminated
Principles can distort attention and cause premature closure; agents should cultivate discernment rather than rely solely on principles
Principles are the only reliable guide for moral action
Agents must follow principles without exception
Principles are useful but only in professional ethics
questions.explain: PA holds that while principles can be useful for guidance, especially in professional ethics, they should not replace discernment. An agent who mechanically applies a rule may miss morally relevant features of the particular case.

questions.q: How is Moral Discernment developed according to the lecture?
options: By memorizing moral rules and principles
Through experience, comparison, reflection, and moral education — learning patterns of relevance from cases
Through passive observation without active reflection
By rejecting all moral learning
By following a single moral authority
questions.explain: Moral Discernment is a trained capacity to notice morally relevant features and understand their relations. It is developed actively through experience, comparison of cases, reflection, and moral education. This endorses learning patterns from cases rather than learning rules mechanically.

questions.q: What analogy does the lecture use to explain how moral concepts might work in particularist theory?
options: Learning mathematics: applying rigid formulas to every problem
Learning a language: we learn how words are used across contexts, not through single definitions applied mechanically
Learning rules: memorizing exceptions and applying them strictly
Learning history: memorizing dates and facts
Learning music: following a single melody exactly
questions.explain: The Practical Grammar analogy compares moral learning to language learning. We learn how words are used across contexts, their grammar, tone, and flexibility. Similarly, moral concepts like cruelty work across contexts in various forms.

questions.q: What is Case Comparison in the particularist method of moral deliberation?
options: Applying the same rule to all similar cases
Comparing similar cases to inform judgment, without mechanically determining later decisions
Rejecting all comparison as subjective
Following the majority decision in similar cases
Using only the most recent case as precedent
questions.explain: Case Comparison is how particularists approach moral deliberation. These comparisons inform judgment but do not mechanically determine later decisions — they cultivate discernment and reveal patterns of relevance.

questions.q: Which statement best captures the particularist objection to Atomistic Specification?
options: Specification makes principles too complex
The extra conditions added to principles are enablers and disablers, not additional reasons, so the principle is not genuinely atomistic
Atomistic Specification is identical to Particularism
Principles should never be added to or modified
There is no particularist objection to this strategy
questions.explain: The particularist makes a technical objection: when a generalist adds conditions, these conditions mix different categories. Conditions like 'the promise was not coerced' are enablers, not additional reasons. This hidden holism undermines the claim to save atomism.

questions.q: According to the lecture, is Particularism compatible with moral generalizations being sometimes true?
options: No, Particularism requires all generalizations to be false
Yes, but true generalizations are not the foundation of moral explanation; principles are not necessary for moral guidance
Yes, and moral generalizations should guide all deliberation
No, Particularism is simply relativism about all moral facts
The lecture does not address this question
questions.explain: Particularism does NOT mean all moral generalizations must be false. Even if generalizations are sometimes true, they are not the foundation of moral explanation. The practical consequence is Principle Abstinence.

questions.q: How do the Generic Generalist Thesis, Universal Relevance Thesis, Polarity Thesis, and Reasons Atomism relate to each other?
options: They are four mutually contradictory positions
Together they form the core generalist position that moral facts are explained by context-independent features with fixed polarity
Only one of them is endorsed by any actual generalist
They directly support Particularism
They are independent and can be mixed freely
questions.explain: The four theses work together to support generalism. Particularists attack all four, but accepting Reasons Holism does not require abandoning all four (as Holistic Generalism shows).

questions.q: In professional ethics contexts, does the lecture suggest that principles are useful?
options: No, professional ethics should never use principles
Yes, principles like informed consent, non-maleficence, and confidentiality provide essential guidance, but should not replace discernment
Yes, and professionals should follow principles without exception
No, professionals should rely only on intuition
Principles are explicitly rejected in all contexts
questions.explain: The particularist position is nuanced: principles are useful for guidance, especially in professional ethics (medical ethics, public service ethics). But principles should not replace discernment — they should guide attention while the agent remains alert to particular features.

questions.q: What is the significance of the exam trap 'Particularism is not moral relativism'?
options: Particularism and relativism are the same thing
Particularism holds features have genuine moral force but that force is context-sensitive, unlike relativism which denies objective moral facts
The exam trap does not apply to this lecture
Particularism denies all moral facts
Relativism accepts moral principles while Particularism rejects them
questions.explain: A central exam trap is confusing Particularism with moral relativism or subjectivism. Particularism holds that moral features have genuine force and objective significance, but that force is context-sensitive.

questions.q: What does the exam trap about silencing versus outweighing emphasize?
options: Silencing and outweighing are the same process
Silenced features have no moral contribution at all, while outweighed features still contribute but insufficiently; they are fundamentally different
Neither silencing nor outweighing occurs in moral reasoning
Silencing makes a feature positive; outweighing makes it negative
The distinction is not important for understanding the lecture
questions.explain: When a feature is silenced, it is simply irrelevant — it has no moral force at all. When a feature is outweighed, it still has moral force (positive or negative) but is insufficient to determine the verdict. This distinction is fundamental.

questions.q: How does Holistic Generalism demonstrate that Reasons Holism does not entail Principle Eliminativism?
options: By proving that Reasons Holism is false
By showing that principles can be reformulated to accommodate context-sensitivity while still functioning as principles
By eliminating all moral principles
By arguing that context is irrelevant to morality
By accepting Principle Eliminativism
questions.explain: Accepting that the moral contribution of a feature depends on context (Reasons Holism) does not logically entail that principles cannot exist (Principle Eliminativism). HG shows principles can be made holistic. The particularist needs a further argument to establish PE.

questions.q: Which of the following best illustrates the difference between a reason and an enabler in the promise case?
options: Both the promise and its lack of coercion are reasons
The promise is the reason; its lack of coercion is an enabler that allows the promise to function as a reason
The lack of coercion is the reason; the promise is merely an enabler
Neither the promise nor its lack of coercion is a moral reason
There is no meaningful difference between them
questions.explain: The real reason is 'I promised.' The fact that the promise was not coerced is not itself a reason — it is a condition that allows the promise to function as a reason. The particularist uses this distinction to argue that Atomistic Specification hides holism.

questions.q: What does the exam trap about PE and PA entailment warn against?
options: Believing that both PE and PA are always true
Assuming that one necessarily follows from the other when they are logically independent positions
Thinking that neither PE nor PA can be true
Confusing moral principles with moral intuitions
Mixing up Generalism and Particularism
questions.explain: PE and PA are logically independent; one does not entail the other. A student might reject PE (holding that some principles exist) while accepting PA (holding that agents should not rely solely on them). Conflating them leads to misidentifying what a particularist is committed to.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes why the distinction between enablers and disablers matters to the particularist argument?
options: Enablers and disablers are not genuine moral concepts
Reasons, enablers, and disablers are completely interchangeable terms
Adding enablers and disablers to a principle disguises holism within a pseudo-atomistic structure, so Atomistic Specification fails
Enablers make principles stronger while disablers make them weaker
The distinction has no relevance to the generalist-particularist debate
questions.explain: This is crucial for understanding why Atomistic Specification fails: the extra conditions added to principles are not additional reasons but enablers/disablers. Since the real reason ('I promised') is separable from the conditions enabling it to function, the principle is not genuinely atomistic — it hides holism inside a pseudo-atomistic structure.
